description_block: The second game of the 1951 Fall Classic would see the mighty Yankees best their cross-river rival N.Y. Giants by a 3-1 score at Yankee Stadium before 66,018 patrons, with Eddie Lopat scattering five hits in a masterful performance. Of utmost significance, this October 5, 1951 contest would not only see the immortal Mickey Mantle stroke his inaugural World Series hit but sadly see “the Mick” carried off the field when his right knee gave out after stepping in a hidden drainage ditch in the top of the fifth inning. Ironically, it would be Willie Mays who hit the baseball to right center field, with the iconic Joe DiMaggio calling off the 19-year-old budding superstar. The Yankee Clipper did make the catch and turned to see his stricken teammate lying in severe pain on the outfield grass. Carried off the field on a stretcher, Mantle was finished for the Series, and although he would return in 1952 to embark on a remarkable career, his unparalleled speed and agility would never be the same. As a grand testament for this historical event, presented here is a PSA 2 Oct. 5, 1951 ticket stub boasting superb aesthetics. Both Yankee insignias have retained their original vibrant hues, the striking bold pink setting encompassing the “BLEACHER ADMISSION” caption boasts virtually all of its original vitality, and the lower end reveals an “extended version” of the stub – a critical aspect for sophisticated ticket enthusiasts. While the Yankees would eventually win the Series in six games, it would be Mantle’s significant game two injury and DiMaggio’s last MLB appearance that would be the indelible highlights of this iconic Fall Classic.

description_block:
One of the most compelling post-WWII rookie cards belongs to the flame throwing Nolan Ryan, with his 1968 Topps #177 inaugural keepsake presented here in a miraculous PSA MINT 9 holder!  Of the 19,000+ PSA encapsulated copies, a fractional 0.36% have managed to achieve the sanctified “9” assessment, and unfathomable to say the least, only a single PSA example boasts the near-impossible GEM MINT 10 grade. Tantamount with this grand offering’s unequivocal stature is Hall of Famer Nolan Ryan's solidified place in baseball history, with the fire-balling right-hander the undisputed record holder for lifetime strikeouts (5,714) and no-hitters (7). His reputation as one of the game's true immortals was solidified when he was voted as the starting pitcher on baseball's team of the century in 1999. His blazing fastball and “nose to toes” curve ultimately enabled the legendary Ryan to claim 324 victories, 61 shutouts (tied with the great Tom Seaver), and 222 complete games over his resounding 27-year career that included eight All-Star nominations. Yet, for all his lofty achievements, his record-setting and extremely stingy 6.6 hits and remarkable 9.5 strikeouts per nine innings will forever stand at or near the top of the charts! He will always be best remembered for his fearsome riding fastball that literally “climbed the ladder” at the hitting zone while consistently exceeding 100 mph in his prime. Indeed, this iconic Hall of Famer struck immense fear into the hearts of baseball’s best hitters who shivered at the sheer thought of digging into the batter’s box against the incomparable Ryan.    
This aesthetically brilliant memento emphatically suffices as one of the finest preserved Ryan rookie cards extant, and its breathtaking condition would prompt even the most sophisticated collector to visualize an ardent youth recently pulling it from a 1968 Topps wax pack at their local “Mom & Pop” store some 58 years ago. Sharing the card with southpaw teammate Jerry Koosman, virtually every attribute bursts with near perfection including crystal-clear clarity, vibrant hues, and blistering sharp edging including four pinpoint corners. Stealing the show is the superior centering, with an abundance of Ryan rookies plagued by poor image positioning. A gleaming obverse side and super clean verso are the final compliments for a card truly meriting its world-class “9” assessment. The naked eye cannot detect any glaring imperfections on its virtually immaculate surfaces, with this timeless heirloom arguably residing as one of the pinnacle Nolan Ryan rookie cards on the planet as well as the perfect testament for his unparalleled MLB tenure. A spectacular memento likewise meriting Cooperstown stature, it joins other iconic Mantle, Mays, Aaron, Clemente, Koufax, Seaver, and Jackson inaugural baseball cards (just to mention a few) as one of the most coveted post-WWII rookie treasures. Its spellbinding eye appeal, regal PSA MINT 9 grade, and first Nolan Ryan sports card image are a truly captivating trifecta substantiating why the elite enthusiast should immediately jump aboard the “Ryan Express” and ride this electrifying keepsake directly to the winners’ circle!

description_block: Spellbinding to say the least, this outstanding SGC 3 VG 1914 T213 Coupon Cigarettes “Type 2” Ty Cobb Portrait suffices as one of the finest eye pleasing copy extant! A “POP 5” SGC marvel, only two SGC examples have managed to achieve a higher assessment. Furthermore, its scarce existence is justified by the COMBINED SGC and PSA census reports listing a mere 93 total examples at the time this was written versus the approximate 4,000 T206 Cobb Red Portrait specimens. Indeed, the total population for the 1914 “Type 2” Coupon Cigarettes Red Portrait Cobb stands at a fractional 2% of its highly populated T206 brethren, with this particular offering boasting spectacular aesthetics for the extremely condition sensitive T213 issue. Due to their wax-like glossy surfaces, most T213 Type 2 subjects reveal obtrusive front side creasing, cracking or other unsightly defects. Certainly not the case for this tobacco dandy that has miraculously defied “father-time” over the past 112 years. From 1910 thru 1919, Coupon Cigarettes release three distinct tobacco card series utilizing similar player images from the classic T206 Tobacco “Monster Set.”  Distinctly known for their various sizes that were typically smaller than a T206 subject as well as the blue ink (as opposed to black) utilized for the player’s name and team, the 2nd Coupon Series was released in 1914 within the Louisiana Region, revealing a “FACTORY No.3 DIST OF LA.” distribution print. The most popular and valuable subject from all three series is the legendary Tyrus Raymond Cobb, still considered by many historians as baseball’s greatest all-time “five tool” player with his record-setting .366 lifetime batting average and 12 batting titles in a 13-year span justify this notion. Cobb’s undisputed stature as a 1936 HOF Charter Member will stand for eternity, and this “Red Portrait” Carl Horner representation of him resides as one of the hobby’s cornerstone cardboard images. Entering the 1914 campaign, the mighty Cobb had already secured a record seven consecutive A.L. batting titles including two .400+ seasons, and his 1914 league-leading .368 figure marked his eight successive title. Not done, the Motor City superstar centerfielder once again paced the Junior Circuit in 1915 to extend his record streak to nine campaigns, with Tris Speaker finally besting Tyrus in 1916. This “heart-stopping” marvel boasts one of the grandest Type 2 Cobb portrait images imaginable, amazingly sidestepping many of the typical surface imperfections prompting lower grades. The well centered iconic portrait pose literally jumps off the card, bolstered by a bold red background and fine resolution. Common with virtually all Type 2 T213’s, the borders exhibit spotty toning, with the even corner wear consistent with most VG-EX examples. For full disclosure, there is a vertical wrinkle situated to the left of the right border, extending through Cobb’s left shoulder and ending near the lower border’s frame. Barely visible to the naked eye, this faint imperfection is only evident upon close scrutiny, certainly not compromising the eye-popping aesthetics of this T213 heirloom. The lower border includes the standard T213 “Cobb, Detroit” blue hued caption, and the final superlative is the relatively clean COUPON CIGARETTES ad back. Of course, it is the immortal Carl Horner “Georgia Peach” central image that takes front and center stage, incredibly maintaining nearly all of its original factory issued features and presenting itself in magnificent fashion!

description_block:
It's an oft-observed, modern-day phenomenon: the cascade of excitement attendant to the emergence of an unopened package, particularly, one that carries the potential of holding desirable and never-touched trading cards. The rarer the pack—and the more precious its possible contents—the better. The sight of a factory-sealed package inevitably provokes a series of conditioned responses. Most immediately, the anxious "What's inside?" reaction, followed by the more deliberately reasoned mental tally of possibilities, and, finally, the compulsion to view the outcome and share in the watching community's resulting enthusiasm. The basic sequence varies by degree and volume of adrenalin expended, depending upon whether the pack in question is 1952 Topps Baseball, 2003-04 Exquisite Collection Basketball, 2026 Topps Baseball Series 1, or whatever else, and the effects are irresistibly contagious. Often, these days, the entire process—from discovery through revelation—is witnessed on live television or broadcast internationally through online media.
Offered here is a simply incredible unopened "find," a national-newsworthy ne plus ultra of the collecting hobby's pack-ripping, content-speculating pastime. This is a virtually never-seen, undisturbed full carton of Sweet Caporal Cigarettes, in all probability dating to the early 20th Century. The dozen smaller units still undisturbed within would have been right at home, ready for sale, on the tobacconist's shelf, circa 1910s-1920s; it's an entirely reasonable expectation that their enticing appearance, were they to be exposed, remains true, to this day.
So, what is likely to be accompanying the faithfully preserved but doubtless now-desiccated cigarettes in each of these dozen packs that have been incubated for more than a century by this magical carton? Informed conjecture suggests (roughly, in descending order of desirability) the following: 1) a T206 "Baseball Series" player insert card, perhaps picturing one of the issue's pantheon of future Hall of Famers), 2) a colorful T59 "Flags of All Nations" insert card, 3) a T34 "Ask Dad ..." advert insert card, or 4) nothing, other than archaeologically profound, combustible tobacco product.
As befits a stand-alone relic of the highest caliber or a fantastic element of a "country store"-themed display, the carton affords a spellbinding presentation. A fragile label on the cardboard box's end affirms content as "1-Dozen 10¢ Packages" of Sweet Caporal-brand cigarettes. A larger, full-length panel accommodates advertising consistent with American Tobacco Co.'s long-running Sweet Caporal campaign evoking the wisdom of family patriarchs: "Ask Dad ... He Knows." (The sentiment's gravity is creatively reinforced in this appeal by a top-hatted silhouette of Abraham Lincoln!) The carton's surfaces reflect more than a century of responsible storage, with very small and insignificant spots of shelf wear posing no meaningful distraction.
Presented here, then, is a piece that stands as a dichotomy delivering boundless enchantment. This carton can be the subject of awe for what it is, and its presence is riveting on the basis of what it could contain. Either perspective, alone, is sufficient to ignite the imagination; taken together, the thoughtful observer can hardly resist the possibilities afforded by this singular, important survivor.

description_block: Offered here is the key Hall of Fame subject emanating from a delightfully obscure, painfully rare issue of periodical premiums. This amazing entry—an elegantly styled portrayal of the demonstrably incomparable Martin Dihigo, rendered on newspaper stock—hails from a Cuban production that circulated in Latin America during the 1946-47 winter league baseball season. The release appeared in two subsets, one featuring 27 Cuban League stars, the other honoring 11 American Major League players (including Ted Williams and Stan Musial). Both types were distributed as inserts in Sensacion periodicals, and both were also available from the publisher in a pair of bound volumes. Martin Dihigo was the greatest of all Cuban baseball players, a paragon athlete who has been recognized by enshrinement in the National Baseball Hall of Fame as well as the Cuban, Mexican, and Dominican Halls. Dihigo excelled as both a pitcher and a hitter (and later, a manager), earning the sobriquet "El Immortal." A Cuban of African descent, Dihigo played for years in the Negro Leagues, appearing for the Cuban Stars, Homestead Grays, Hilldale Giants, and New York Cubans over his 22-year career in the States. He also toiled in the Cuban and Mexican leagues, earning four Cuban League MVP awards. In one season in Mexico, with Veracruz, Dihigo compiled an 18-2 record and 0.92 ERA, while also winning the batting title with a .387 average. He played every single position on the diamond, frequently hitting for an average in the high .300s. Dihigo could not be intimidated on the mound or at the plate, as evidenced by one famous duel in the Mexican heat against Satchel Paige. With the score tied at 1-1 going into the ninth inning, Paige succumbed to the heat and the pressure, reluctantly leaving the game only to see his reliever give up a walkoff home run to Dihigo—the starting pitcher for the opposition in the contest. This remarkable tribute item exhibits an extraordinarily impressive presentation that suitably honors a one-of-a-kind competitor of Dihigo's stature. The obverse's sublime, softly colored likeness illuminates the player's facial features and Cienfuegos uniform details from within a decorative frame. On the back, the piece delivers a lengthy and thorough, lifetime statistical report to accompany a brief but informative biography. Readily observable evidence of past circulation is limited to inconsequential wear (and one tiny chip) at the delicate, rough-cut edges. This is a showpiece collectible, celebrating a memorable ballplayer who possessed a sterling character to accompany otherworldly talents.

description_block:
Hall of Famer. An 11-piece collection of 1916 BF2 Ferguson Bakery baseball felt pennant collectibles is presented. The approximately 2-7/8-by-6-inch cloth souvenirs feature small, 1-1/4-by-1-3/4-inch, black-and-white player photos—the same images seen on cards made by The Sporting News during this period—appliquéd to the felt on their front surfaces. White or black appliqués also served to identify player and team names, plus decorative embellishments, to complement the items' photographs. This collection holds 11 different designs (including one player pictured twice, but on two different-colored felt backings).
An incredible roster of ballplayers is revealed in this small but powerful BF2 lineup. Foremost, of course, is the centerpiece in the person of Joe Jackson. (Inevitably, the oxygen leaves the room, palpitations ensue in enthusiasts' hearts, and no attention is paid elsewhere for anxious moments whenever a career-contemporary memento of "Shoeless Joe" is spotted.) The gallery's four Cooperstown-enshrined figures—Eddie Collins, Charles Comiskey, Urban Faber, Ray Schalk—add serious star-power. Upon another, broader look, the group seems to constitute a preview of the 1919 A.L. pennant winners, who came to be known, of course, as the "Black Sox." Even "Chic" Gandil, shown with the Indians, was destined to join the Pale Hose franchise.
BF2's formidable scarcity adds yet another facet to these attractive survivors' appeal. In 1916, a penny for a piece of candy and a card represented a serious expenditure. A nickel for a loaf of bread, in order to obtain a ballplayer souvenir? That flight of fancy could only have been subsidized by Mom, and the transaction launched to capture a BF2 thus became something between a diffident plea and a test of wills. Finally, Roxbury, Mass., home of the bakery that sponsored the pennants, was a tiny outpost, relatively speaking, and other time-zones weren't, and have never been, known to experience inundation in BF2s. The arrival of this quality sampling, then, is a truly special event.
These 11 felt pennants generally present at the EX to EX/MT level with occasional spots of light toning and very minor peripheral faults. Their uniformly clear photo components display mostly EX/MT character with few readily observable discrepancies,

condition_note: Minor, peripheral imperfections

description_block:
Graded EX-MT 6 by PSA (15194498), one of just four copies in this configuration placed at that level with only one graded higher. Presented is a clean ticket stub from the July 4, 1923 heavyweight title bout between undisputed champion Jack Dempsey and challenger Tommy Gibbons in Shelby, Montana. After having remained dormant for two years following his era-defining knockout of Georges Carpentier in 1921, "The Manassa Mauler" reentered the ring against Gibbons for a heavyweight title fight that doubled as a boom opportunity for the town of Shelby, which harbored hopes of becoming an economic hub after the recent discovery of oil in the area. A tactical affair, Dempsey picked Gibbons apart over 15 rounds and won by decision (the result was less positive for Shelby, which nearly went bankrupt as a result of sluggish ticket sales, a circumstance largely attributable to high prices). Dempsey fought just four more times in his career, retiring at the age of 32 after a famous bout with Gene Tunney. This paper relic concedes a handful of minor, peripheral imperfections, but its detailed, intricate art style is clearly and conspicuously displayed.

card_name: 1917 E135 Collins-McCarthy #80 Rogers Hornsby Rookie Card
condition_note: Slight manual trims along the upper and right edges.
special_note: Super-scarce rookie card, highly coveted, and significant in the rookie card world.
description_block: Super-scarce, the 1917 Collins McCarthy Rogers Hornsby inaugural cardboard subject truly stands as one of the most highly coveted rookie cards extant. Presented here just happens to be one of the finest visually pleasing copies, an SGC “Authentic” marvel that joins a mere 13 other Collins McCarthy ad back examples (in any grade) on the prestigious SGC census report. PSA lists only five additional specimens, truly substantiating its bona fide paucity level. In 1917 the Collins McCarthy Candy Co. produced a 200-card set almost identical to the Boston Store Clothier and Standard Biscuit Bread Co. issues. With cards of the incomparable Babe Ruth, “Shoeless” Joe Jackson, Ty Cobb and Honus Wagner included in the set, many of the other prominent Cooperstown inductees fall short of the full recognition they surely merit including the great Rogers Hornsby’s first cardboard issue. Tantamount with this offering’s spellbinding aesthetics is the “Rajah’s” unparallelled batting prowess, since most baseball experts consider the immortal Hornsby our National Pastime’s premier all-time right-handed hitter. Statistically speaking, Hornsby’s numbers certainly support that notion with six consecutive batting titles, a .358 lifetime average, the highest modern-day National League average (.424 in 1924), and most incredibly, averaging .400 over 5 consecutive seasons (1921 – 1925)! Considering his remarkable batting accomplishments, Hornsby has not received much adoration, making him an extremely underrated baseball immortal. In 1915, he would make only 61 plate appearances in St, Louis, with the following 1916 campaign being his first full season. Hornsby wouldn’t disappoint the Redbird fans, posting a .313 average, the first of 21 campaigns the multi-position infielder would surpass the exalted .300 mark. While a few Hornsby caramel, exhibit and strip cards exist from his peak value years (1920 – 1925), other than his scarce M101-6 Felix Mendelsohn subject, there are no other mainstream pre-1920 Hornsby issues. This justifies why his 1917 rookie card is such an illustrious artifact. The Hornsby offering provides a classic black & white throwing image (vs. hitting), with his position listed as “1st Base” as opposed to his legendary second sacker position. The illustration proudly portrays crystal-clear clarity, unimprovable contrast as well as strong square corners exhibiting subtle wear, and most significantly, the relatively fine centering only reveals a modest favoritism towards the right edge. This is an excruciatingly tough attribute to find, with most of the 1917 Hornsby E135 issues plagued by extremely poor image positioning. Atypically, no obtrusive surface defects are evident, with the only notable imperfections being a few diminutive soling spots along the upper right border, general surface toning/wear, and a faint scratch near the “E” in “ROGERS” - barely visible to the naked eye. The final superlatives are the bold “ROGERS HORNSBY – 1st B. – St. Louis Cardinals – 80” caption along the lower border and a relatively clean Collins McCarthy ad back. For full disclosure, it appears the “Authentic” assessment is due to ever so slight manual trims along the upper and right edges, with these minimal alterations not compromising the overall integrity of the card. Regardless, the critical aspect of this museum worthy offering is its outstanding eye appeal and utmost rarity, a momentous “dynamic duo.” Previously undervalued, vintage rookie card enthusiasts are now catching on to its scarce existence and earth-shattering significance in the rookie card world, substantiated by a PSA 4 nailing down $55K in 2023 and a low-grade SGC 1.5 recently fetching $22K in a private sale. Although rendering an “Authentic” assessment, this world-class heirloom emanates aesthetics in the mid-grade range, boasting immense future prosperity while standing as the perfect testament for the great “Rajah’s” resounding legacy!

description_block: Offered is a vintage 1923 New York Yankees old Yankee Stadium bleacher seat from "The House That Ruth Built." The Columbia-blue painted wood slats and iron stanchion, with the seat measuring 22.5-by-31.5-by-9 inches, exhibit heavy wear from use. The number "7" is stenciled on the top of the front slat. The original Yankee Stadium, located in The Bronx, New York, was the home ballpark of the New York Yankees from 1923 to 1973 and then from 1976 to 2008. The stadium hosted 6,581 Yankees regular-season home games during its 85-year history. It was also the home of the New York Giants National Football League team from 1956 through the first part of the 1973–74 NFL season. The ballpark was renovated after the 1973 season, re-opening in 1976, and closed after the 2008 Major League Baseball season. The original Yankee Stadium was demolished in 2010, two years after it closed, and the 8-acre site was converted into a public park called Heritage Field. This is a thrilling memento from one of the most celebrated ballparks in all of MLB, and perhaps in all of sports - a seat originally affixed to an area visited by a vast number of colossal long balls courtesy of the greatest Yankee immortals including Ruth, Gehrig, DiMaggio and Mantle!

card_name: 1914-15 Minor League Team Original Cabinet Photograph
condition_note: The cardboard mount shows decades' worth of physical misfortune, while the picture has relatively inconsequential disturbances.
special_note: Earliest known professional baseball image of Rogers Hornsby.
description_block: This rare and remarkable vintage photograph captures the youthful likeness of a very young. future National Baseball Hall of Famer: Rogers Hornsby. Ah, small-town baseball, a calling that was notable for scenes captured for posterity which include as many animals, children, and puffed-up local dignitaries as ballplayers! The soon-to-be star, Hornsby, is shown in a magnificently clear image that caught an impressive assembly posed in front of the local firehouse; an ink inscription in the photo's bottom margin reads, "Pride of Denison," and, clearly, that's exactly what these folks were. (It must be kept in mind that, during this period, quality souvenirs of this type were almost never created, and less likely, still, to have survived the succeeding century-plus span of cultural activity.) In 1914, Hornsby played for these "Denison Champions" of the Class D Texas-Oklahoma League in Denison, Texas. (Unfortunately, statistics from this interlude are not available.) By 1915, the aspiring ballplayer was toiling for the "Denison Railroaders" of the Class D Western Association, the organization from which he was summoned to the St. Louis Cardinals later that season. For the Railroaders, he batted .277 in 119 games (posting 429 at-bats) with 119 hits, 24 stolen bases, 4 homers, 26 doubles, 75 runs scored, and a .375 slugging percentage. In concluding 1915 (18 games with the big-league club), the future star batted an underwhelming .246, but this preceded a breakout year in 1916. In that campaign, Hornsby posted a .313 batting average to formally embark upon a career that would arguably place him as the National Pastime’s greatest all-time right-handed hitter! This phenomenal paper heirloom—dating to the very first moments of the much-lauded Hornsby's career in professional baseball—reveals the practical design of the period's cabinet-style studio images. The piece's cardboard mount, which was fashioned in the interest of protecting the cabinet's delicate photo component, shows the decades'-worth of physical misfortune by which the relic was imperiled, while the most significant element—the picture, itself—is bothered only by relatively inconsequential disturbances (most notably, right-side corner faults and a lower-right-aspect wrinkle that touches just horses, not people). An unforgettable antique and, quite possibly, a one-of-a-kind survivor!

card_name: 1954 Joe DiMaggio, Marilyn Monroe Newlyweds Type I Original Photo
condition_note: Retaining most of its original eye-popping attributes for the past 72 years.
special_note: This photo captures the iconic marriage of Joe DiMaggio and Marilyn Monroe, a significant cultural moment in American history.
description_block: Not even Hollywood could produce a better script than the marriage of Joe DiMaggio and Marilyn Monroe on January 14, 1954, after an 18-month courtship that began the year after “Joltin’ Joe” hung up his baseball cleats forever. This extraordinary Type 1 photo portrays both DiMaggio and Monroe on their newsworthy honeymoon, conducting a press conference at the renowned Imperial Hotel in Tokyo, Japan. Their iconic marriage captivated the entire Nation, with this storybook couple a miraculous-like global feature. America’s legendary “blonde bombshell”, Marilyn Monroe was born Norma Jean Mortenson on June 1, 1926, eventually changing her name and becoming America’s greatest all-time sex symbol. Indeed, Monroe was the true embodiment of an American culture widely changing its attitude towards sexuality throughout the 1950’s, with her ultra-controversial nude centerfold picture in Playboy’s inaugural 1953 issue prompting this newly adapted mindset. Her extensive list of films would gross over $200 million, and by the time of her tragic death in 1962, she would arguably stand alongside the likes of Elvis Presley and Frank Sinatra as America’s most popular Hollywood entertainers. While equally popular on the playing field and one of baseball’s greatest all-time players, the Yankee Clipper carried a more tranquil personality, never seeking public attention and painstakingly choosing a rather quiet lifestyle. Tantamount to his new bride, “Joe D.” was likewise a virtual cult hero, worshiped by millions who were fascinated by his near-flawless play and record-setting 56-game hitting streak in 1941. Unfortunately, their oppositive personalities led to a rather brief marriage, with Marilyn filing for divorce less than a year after their wedding date. DiMaggio would always retain his true love for Marilyn, and after her untimely death, placed roses on her grace three times a week for some 20 years. This extremely scarce U.S. Army Corps photo is a magnificent testimony for this seemingly fairytale couple, retaining most of its original eye-popping attributes for the past 72 years.

special_note: Includes MBA Silver Diamond Certification, one of only three PSA 8.5 copies.
description_block:
Tantamount to the immortal legacy of the incomparable Roberto Clemente is this extraordinary PSA 8.5 NM-MT+ 1955 Topps rookie card boasting the most significant MBA Silver Diamond Certification. Joined by only two other PSA copies at this extremely rare plateau, a meager twelve examples have been graded higher! One of the finest of its kind, we cannot imagine any of the 11 PSA 9's besting the immaculate-like aesthetics of this miraculous offering, with its awe-inspiring eye appeal and technical attributes rightfully meriting the critical MBA Silver Diamond Sticker. It has been some four years since a PSA 8.5 publicly sold, with prior pricing points rendered virtually irrelevant over that extensive time span. However, as an effective benchmark, one of the PSA 9s breeched $1 million only last year (the third PSA 9 copy to achieve the seven-figure-plus mark), justifying the immense value of a high-grade Clemente rookie card. Even more important is the fact that this timeless heirloom portrays the near-impossible to find virtually perfect positioned image (nearly 50/50), with the centering for most of the existing PSA 9s inferior to this cardboard anomaly. It therefore comes with little surprise that this Cooperstown worthy offering achieved the highly coveted MBA Silver Diamond Certification, and as elite collectors surely know, these prized stickers validate the superior visual appeal for the grade, ultimately leading to vast pricing premiums in public auctions.
Along with the exalted 1951 Bowman Mantle and Mays issues, no post-1950s rookie card is more valuable than the illustrious 1955 Topps Roberto Clemente inaugural subject. No limits are seemingly in sight for its substantial pricing escalation, with the 1955 Clemente one of the most desirable and esteemed collectibles extant. Its inception can be traced back to when the Brooklyn Dodgers signed Clemente in the February 1954 amateur draft, assigning him to play with the celebrated Montreal Royals. After a single season with Montreal, the Pirates would eventually select Clemente in the rookie draft, signing the star right-fielder on November 22, 1954. Clemente would capture a championship with the 1954-55 Cangrejeros club, and made his MLB debut on April 17, 1955, posting his first MLB hit in a 10-3 Pirates loss to the Brooklyn Dodgers at Forbes Field. Although his rookie season would see the future Cooperstown inductee bat only .255 on a last-place club, his cannon-like throwing arm, hitting, fielding, and base-running skills electrified the Pittsburgh faithful who were smitten by his flashes of brilliance. It was these world class traits that would prompt the prestigious Topps Chewing Gum Co. to issue his #164 inaugural baseball card as part of their glorified 1955 set, with the hallowed #164 Clemente subject now etched in stone as one of the most celebrated post-WWII cards.
The unparalleled mystique of any Clemente rookie card, let alone one of the two known PSA 8.5s should be highly expected, especially considering Roberto's legendary status amongst the Hispanic baseball community being synonymous with the magnitude of Jackie Robinson's legacy to Black Americans. Clemente's incredible accomplishments include a .317 lifetime batting average, 3,000 career hits, the 1966 regular season NL MVP award, four batting titles, 12 consecutive Gold Glove awards, and if that doesn't whet your appetite, in 1971 he won the World Series MVP when he dominated the Baltimore Orioles via his magnificent hitting and fielding prowess. Yet, as is the case with the immortal Lou Gehrig, he will always be best remembered for his tragic death when, after the 1972 season, his plane crashed into the Atlantic Ocean carrying supplies to assist earthquake victims in Nicaragua. His legacy far surpasses most post-WWII Cooperstown inductees, with his iconic 1955 Topps issue on virtually every world-class collector’s bucket list. Like his uncanny playing brilliance is this remarkable offering that appears as if a captivated "Steel City" youth has just been pulled it from a 1955 wax pack. A sparkling front side boasts the legendary portrait and batting poses that proudly reveal unimprovable clarity and contrast, as well as reflecting a host of robust hues. Yet, as previously stated, it is the near-perfect centering that truly "steals the show," with most Clemente rookie cards plagued by severely skewed images. Razor sharp corner tips, fine edging, and pack-fresh surfaces are the final exclamation points for this bona fide cardboard "blazer" that arguably resides as one of the hobby's finest preserved copies. Virtually every technical attribute is consistent with sheer perfection, and even the most meticulous enthusiasts might agree that a PSA 9 assessment would surely coincide with its world-class qualities and appearance. The legendary Roberto Clemente coined the eloquent quote: "Any time you have an opportunity to make a difference in this world, and you don't, then you are wasting your time on Earth," living his sanctified life on earth to the tune of that hallowed notion. No truer words were ever spoken by even the most articulate of world philosophers, and it is apropos that the immortal Clemente would utter such a quote for he represented the embodiment of human valor. Ironically, it would be his courageous actions that would tragically cut his life short when the aforementioned plane crash claimed his life on December 31, 1972. He was loved by so many, and even one of his dearest friends, Pirates catcher Manny Sanguillen, missed Clemente’s memorial service, choosing instead to dive into the Atlantic Ocean's frigid waters in an unsuccessful effort to find his beloved teammate. It is therefore with bittersweet irony that for all of Roberto Clemente's world-class achievements, this Hall of Famer's legacy will forever be linked to his heroic death, and we cannot imagine a finer testament for his iconic stature than this "POP 3" PSA 8.5 rookie card including the momentous MBA Silver Diamond Certification!

About Graded Magazines: PSA and CGC are the two major grading companies in the fast-growing Graded Magazine space. Both grade on a scale of 10 that generally tops out at 9.8 for vintage magazines but may reach 9.9 or even 10.0 for modern magazines. The all-time record price for a "Newsstand" Graded Magazine (never mailed, no address label) is the $229,000 paid for a Pop 1, PSA 9.6, 1983 Sports Illustrated Michael Jordan 1st Cover. The corresponding record for a high-grade "Subscription" Graded Magazine (mailed, with address label intact or removed) is the $20,000 paid for a Pop 2, CGC 9.6, 1984 Sports Illustrated Michael Jordan 1st Pro Cover. Newsstand copies are considered the far rarer, more sought-after gold standard. Subscription copies that have survived the mail in ultra-high grade may also command premium value. Debut magazine appearances, such as "1st Cover," "1st Solo Cover" and "1st Pro Cover" are viewed by collectors as extra-valuable rookie cards. Pop Reports from the PSA Census and CGC Census are accurate at the time a lot is posted for auction yet are subject to change. Grader Notes on condition can often be found there. Examples of typical condition flaws include creases; bends; tears; stains; dents; ripples; spine ticks; fingerprints; erasures; tanning; discoloration; and missing/partial pages. Magazine "cleaning/pressing" is an acceptable practice to remove some defects (such as creases that don't break color) and improve condition. PSA and CGC both offer pressing services. Slabs/holders may also bear incidental streaks, marks, scratches, interior spots and other handling wear. condition_note: Loose fibers at the top edge do not disturb Marquard's image.
special_note: Tobacco silks are unusual, seldom-encountered treasures.
description_block: Graded GD 2 by BVG (0005283807). Hall of Famer. An extraordinarily visual item, this satiny survivor employs the likeness of all-time great Rube Marquard as borrowed from its issuer's magnificent T205 Gold Border series. The precise, well-defined line drawing used to recreate the portrayal, here, is well-preserved on this example, and its original "Turkey Red Cigarettes" backpaper remains securely attached. Loose fibers at the top edge (as typically seen in this delicate issue) do not disturb Marquard's image. It must be mentioned that tobacco silks are unusual, seldom-encountered treasures, and they're sometimes misunderstood by non-specialists when condition assessments are rendered. Specifically, a horizontal line at the reverse-side midpoint of an item is often and rationally interpreted as a "crease," but on an S74 White Silk's backpaper, the same attribute is properly termed "factory-induced packaging fold." Further, third-party graders' census reporting doesn't typically distinguish between S74 Silks White (which bear fragile, printed-paper backing) and S72 Silks Colored (which were distributed in backless form). Obverse display quality of this admirable memento is far superior to what is suggested by the item's assigned grade.

description_block: Not even Hollywood could produce a more fascinating script than the 1951 MLB campaign that saw two of our National Pastime’s greatest centerfielders take the “Big Apple” by storm. Joining Brooklyn’s Duke Snider on baseball’s grandest stage, both Willie Mays and Mickey Mantle would be embarking on careers for the ages, with the immortal “Say Hey Kid” arguably dubbed baseball’s greatest “five-tool” player. This exhilarating 19-year-old rookie could hit, run, throw and field with the best of them, ultimately ending his iconic 23-year tenure with 660 homers, 1909 R.B.I.’s, 3,218 safeties, a record 24 All-Star nods, two MVP Awards, 12 Gold Gloves, and a 1954 world championship when his electrifying game one “over the shoulder” catch in the deepest confines of centerfield set the stage for New York’s four-game sweep of the Cleveland Indians. As a grand testament for that glorious 1951 rookie campaign, presented here is a “heart-stopping” PSA Authentic 1951 Bowman #305 signed rookie card boasting an extremely bold PSA NM 7 autograph. Presenting itself far superior to the rather harsh assessment, the imposing blue sharpie script emanates conservative “8” strength, affixed to Willie’s undisputed inaugural MLB subject. Finding any Willie Mays autographed Bowman rookie is no easy chore, with PSA listing only 38 scripted copies at the time this was written. Most significantly, the total signed Mays rookies represent only 1.5% of the 2,500+ unsigned examples, a mere fraction of his highly populated unscripted rookie card. Previously undervalued, collectors are recently “catching on” to the significant future prosperity of a signed Mays rookie, substantiated by a staggering $220K December 2025 sale from the Golden Age collection and  most likely resetting the market value for this Cooperstown worthy heirloom. The 1951 campaign would see Mays labor right from the start, going hitless in his first 24 at-bats before ending the drought with a mammoth homer off legendary HOF southpaw Warren Spahn. Willie would end the season with a stellar .274 batting average and 20 dingers, ably assisting the Giants in capturing the N.L. Pennant. Before his untimely passing on June 18, 2024, Mays was considered baseball’s greatest living player, and his unparalleled ability to play every facet of the game as good or superior to any of his peers lead many historians to give him the nod as the finest player to ever grace a baseball diamond. The card itself reveals “GD-VG” aesthetics, highlighted by its vivid resolution, lack of vertical print lines, vibrant hues and near-impossible to find superior image positioning. Indeed, most Mays rookie cards are plagued by skewed images, with this extreme anomaly sidestepping this typical stigma. Imperfections include even corner wear, numerous stray creases, and some diminutive surface snow, none of which detracting from the splendid central image. Of course, it is the bold blue sharpie “Willie Mays” script perfectly affixed across his while flannels that truly “steals the show.” It is seemingly incomprehensible to imagine the hallowed “Say Hey Kid” once held this card in his hands, taking the time to place his majestic autograph on this timeless memento. While Mays is no longer with us, this outstanding autographed 1951 Bowman subject proudly keeps his spirit alive, standing tall as one of the most sought-after autographed rookie cards on the planet!

condition_note: Beyond magnificent in all aspects of condition sensitivity.
special_note: Possibly sufficing as the optimum 1957 Topps Mantle on the planet.
description_block: Goldin Auctions is proud to present one of the finest of all 1957 Topps #95 Mickey Mantle subjects, an extraordinary PSA MINT 9 copy that, from a pure aesthetics perspective, arguably stands at the pinnacle of the hobby as the most visually pleasing copy! Only bested by a single example, we cannot imagine any of the other PSA 9s or even the sole PSA 10 specimen besting this time-tested marvel that miraculously includes near-perfect 50/50 image positioning as well as zero image "tilt." Indeed, the classic Mantle batting pose boasts virtually perfect alignment, a near-impossible endeavor for any 1957 Topps card, let alone the incomparable #95 Mickey subject. One of the major stigmas for the 1957 Topps series is their unsightly skewed images via poor factory cuts, consistently plagued by unruly image "tilts" as well as obtrusive positioning between the four borders. This "unique for the eye appeal" offering has successfully defied all odds, and we cannot imagine any of the other 21 PSA MINT 9 copies or even the sole PSA 10 matching up to this Cooperstown worthy keepsake’s compelling aesthetics. The $12.6 million sale of an SGC 9.5 MT+ 1952 Topps Mantle in August 2022, the highest amount ever paid for a sports card in a public auction, substantiated the notion that "the Mick" rules the post-WWII card market. Mantle's HOF credentials are seemingly countless including 536 home runs, three MVPs, twelve pennants, seven world championships, a World Series Home Run record (18), and a Triple Crown season in 1956. Following that "Cinderella" '56 campaign in which the Yankees also reclaimed the world championship, Topps issued one of the "Commerce Comets" most popular cards in 1957, with the mighty Mick ultimately capturing his second consecutive MVP award that same season. It was five years ago that an inferior 9 sold for $210K, and while certainly a formidable example, it could not match the unparalleled presentation of this "heart-stopping" anomaly that stakes a claim as the premier ’57 Topps Mantle. The phrase "a sure thing" is seldom used, yet high-grade Mantle cards continue to escalate in value at an alarming rate, reaffirming that the "Oklahoma Kid" continues to be one of the cornerstones of the illustrious market. The way Mantle secured this stranglehold on the card collecting circuit remains a mystery. Was it the mystique of his 1952 Topps rookie card, being the great Joe DiMaggio's successor, or simply his long tape-measure home runs that could test the confines of Yellowstone Park? Whatever the reason, his cards hold a special place next to the great pre-war sluggers such as Ruth, Cobb, Wagner, Jackson, and Gehrig, with this 1957 museum-quality example proudly standing tall as one of Mantle's grandest cardboard keepsakes. The card itself is beyond magnificent in all aspects of condition sensitivity, highlighted by the previously mentioned nearly "spot-on" 50/50 centering that has also sidestepped any noticeable "tilt." Additional world-class attributes include the crystal-clear and richly hued Mantle batting image as he possibly clouts another one of his majestic long balls donning the classic Yankee pinstripes. Dazzling white borders lead to a blistering sharp perimeter and four pinpoint corners that could actually draw blood. Both the front and back surfaces are immaculate, with the critical obverse side boasting its original glossy luster. Indeed, it is an excruciating task to locate this 69-year-old memento including its factory issued sheen, a resounding compliment to its previous owners who meticulously preserved this cardboard heirloom at the highest level. The naked eye cannot detect any notable imperfections, and the final "thumbs up" is the verso's bold and vivid red and blue typography. Considering the lofty seven and eight figure price tags prices for MINT 9 1951 Bowman and 1952 Topps Mantles, respectively, the sophisticated collector may need to place their focus on some of the six-figure 1950s Mantle issues, such as this remarkable '57 Topps offering—before their values breach a higher plateau. Possibly sufficing as the optimum 1957 Topps Mantle on the planet and issued during one of his greatest campaigns whereby "the Mick" claimed his second MVP Award, we will defer to the meticulous collector to ultimately determine the unprecedented true worth for this incomparable "best of the best" heirloom!

special_note: This card is recognized as one of the most illustrious post-WWII issues and has immense pricing upticks.
description_block:
The momentous $12.6 million sale of a 1952 Topps #311 Mickey Mantle SGC GEM MINT 9.5 copy in August 2022 electrified the hobby, putting the collecting community on notice as to the unlimited investment potential of any high-grade ’52 Topps #311 high-number subject. While not a GEM MINT example, this outstanding SGC NM 7 marvel likewise offers an abundance of pack-fresh qualities for “the Mick’s” inaugural Topps card. Goldin’s recent February 2026 Vintage Auction produced a record-setting $732K sale for an SGC 7.5 example, and after completely scouring this pack-fresh offering, the only notable technical attribute advantage versus the 7.5 example was its somewhat superior image positioning. Several “NM 7” copies have surpassed the $400K mark and considering the continuous escalated pricing of the ’52 Topps Mantle in ANY GRADE, we cannot even begin to estimate the potential value of this remarkable offering.  Even low grade ’52 Topps Mantles are realizing immense sales including PSA 3.5 and PSA 3 specimens nailing down record-breaking $244K and $240K pricing points, respectively. Of course, the assessment and visual appeal are the key factors in determining its ultimate value, and this sensational keepsake checks both critical boxes – a truly resounding dynamic duo. Most significantly, while Mantle’s iconic image does favor the right edge, it has successfully eluded any severe “tilt”, with a vast number of these subjects consistently plagued by unsightly skewed illustrations. The unparalleled mystique of the ‘52 Topps Mantle is directly linked to Topps Chewing Gum Co. owner Sy Berger’s decision to dump “truckloads” of excess 1952 Topps high-number vending cases into the Atlantic’s murky waters off the coast of New Jersey, prompting the “birth” of the ’52 Topps Mantle’s majestic character. This historic baseball card stands tall as our hobby’s most illustrious post-WWII issue while proudly shining forth like a beacon of light, with its uncontested popularity the main driver of its tsunami-like pricing surge.  
Issued the year after “Joltin’ Joe” DiMaggio completed his final MLB campaign; this landmark 1952 Topps high-number subject would set the stage for a booming “post-war” card market led by the legendary Mantle. Who would have possibly thought that the exodus of the immortal Yankee Clipper would lead to the beginning of yet another celebrated career, with the “Joe D.” passing the torch to a powerful 19-year-old slugger from Commerce, Oklahoma named Mickey Charles Mantle. After being sent down to the minor leagues in July 1951 due to a horrific slump, Mantle would return to the big leagues in August to embark on one of the most celebrated careers in MLB history. His immediate star stature would prompt the innovative Topps Chewing Gum Co. to include Mickey as the #311 subject in their landmark 1952 Topps set, the inaugural card appearing in the esteemed ’52 Topps high-number series. The stage was now set for this Mantle issue to leave an indelible mark on the card collecting circuit, with this future Hall of Famer eventually recognized as the true embodiment of a national hero. After an “up and down” 1951 rookie campaign, Mantle would begin to put it all together in 1952, the year his Topps card was issued. Batting a stellar .311, he would also clout 23 round-trippers while knocking in 87 runs, a bona fide sign of things to come for this supernatural-like phenom. His unmatched power would lead to him blasting at least 10 horsehide spheres into the grandstands at distances exceeding 500 feet; he hit two majestic home runs off the Yankee Stadium’s right field façade; and still owns the MLB record for the furthest home run when in 1953 he walloped a Chuck Stobbs fastball completely out of Griffith’s Stadium at an unprecedented 565 feet! The incomparable Mantle hit a baseball harder and further than anyone who ever graced a batter’s box, and the phenomenon of his incredible tape-measure home runs that could literally test the confines of any ballpark has spilled over to his high-grade 1952 Topps subjects that emphatically reflect unlimited future prosperity.
The 1952 Topps Mantle’s sudden rise to stardom in the late 1980’s ably assisted the card market’s unequivocal stature, with its unrestrained pricing points redefining one’s perspective for utilizing sports cards as viable investment options. The 1952 Topps Mantle currently boasts immense pricing upticks, justified by the aforementioned sales of eye pleasing copies. One look at this spine-tingling bubble gum card could prompt even the most meticulous enthusiast to “skip a beat”, with its myriad of “blazer” qualities stubbornly defying father-time over the past 74 years. The classic “bat over shoulder” pose reflects a vibrant azure-blue setting successfully eluding commonly seen surface snow, and for full disclosure, there is an extremely faint area of toning situated along the upper left frame. You can literally feel Mickey’s curious nature as he gazes into the unknown future with his rich yellow bat situated over his right shoulder, displaying a youthful innocence that would eventually lead to his incredible Yankees legacy. Crystal-clear clarity, sparkling facial hues, the absence of any glaring blemishes on either side, bright white borders, relatively clean borders, right angled corners revealing only diminutive aging, and a clean verso all combine to substantiate the hallowed near-mint grade. While the off-positioned “side to side” centering prevents a higher assessment, the image boasts near-perfect “top to bottom” positioning. The final superlatives are the immaculate-like Yankees logo and vivid Mickey Mantle text box likewise justifying the sanctified “7” grade. Awe-inspiring to say the least, this captivating “Commerce Comet” cardboard wonder proudly portrays a global cornerstone image, with only the T206 Honus Wagner “Holy Grail” possibly besting its unparallelled popularity!

This candy treat is extra special because the immortal HOF first sacker was only issued in 1914, with Chance excluded from the 1915 set due to his retirement after the 1914 season (Chance managed the Yankees during the 1914 campaign). Ironically, he was replaced by standout first sacker Hal “Prince” Chase in the 1915 set, with Chase inexplicably omitted from the 1914 issue. This Cooperstown Inductee’s immense popularity stems from being the final cog in the iconic “Tinker to Evers to Chance” double-play combination, with the fiery “Windy City” captain leading the Cubbies to two consecutive world championships in 1907-08. The immortal Chance’s brilliant portrait pose literally jumps off the card, boasting outstanding resolution and contrast while being flanked by a flaming red setting. As is the case with most 1914 Cracker Jacks, accounting for the grade are various areas of caramel corn staining, in this case along the upper right and lower left borders as well as on the verso. While some lighter staining is also apparent on Chance’s New York Americans Jersey, it is the captivating portrait pose and strong mid-grade corners that truly “steal the show”. The final superlative is the absence of any severe creasing, with this offering’s ultra-thin cardboard stock sidestepping the typical wrinkles and surface damage plaguing most of these fragile keepsakes. Most significantly, considering the 1914 Frank Chance subject was omitted from the 1915 series, this esteemed heirloom will forever stand as one of the most exalted 1914 Cracker Jacks!

description_block: This majestic Team Composite rendering exhibits 18 portrait likenesses revealing individual members of the 1905 Cleveland Base Ball Club. The 13-by-14-inch pieces from the W601 release were distributed–for ten cents per Composite–by Sporting Life, an American weekly newspaper that provided national coverage on sports (focusing on baseball and trap shooting); they were also made available as string-bound sets, accounting for the three neat, as-made holes in this relic's left-side margin. Sporting Life was a direct competitor to The Sporting News, and by 1890 it was one of the most widely circulated sporting- or baseball-themed periodicals in the country. The publication also released the M116 series of baseball cards in 1910-11, as well as the famous W600 Cabinet series of 1902-11. The Composite of the Cleveland "Naps" offered here is highlighted by Hall of Fame teammates Napoleon Lajoie, Addie Joss, and Elmer Flick. This nicely preserved paper heirloom concedes routine traces of mild toning, and presents with clean grandeur. Overall presentation quality is minimally EX/MT.

description_block: The 1936 season would see the Yankees call up their star centerfielder Joseph Paul DiMaggio and he would quickly join Yankee captain Lou Gehrig in leading the Yankees to their first World Series appearance since 1932. Led by six Cooperstown Inductees on the playing field (Gehrig, DiMaggio, Dickey, Ruffing, Lazzeri, and Gomez) as well as their Hall of Fame owner (Col. Jacob Ruppert), manager (Joe McCarthy) and coach (Earl Combs); the Yankees would win 102 games and coast to the American League Pennant. The Fall Classic would then see the Bronx Bombers capture the first of four consecutive championships, besting the New York Giants in six games. This 1936 Yankees PSA Type 1 Underwood & Underwood Photo stands as the perfect testament for that incomparable team, revealing the Polo Grounds visiting dugout with Gehrig situated on the far left and “Joltin’ Joe” 10th from the left. These two baseball immortals combined to have a sensational campaign, with a rookie “Yankee Clipper” and the slugging “Iron Horse” combining to terrorize American League hurlers to the tune of 78 round-trippers and 277 R.B.I.’s!  Indeed, it certainly appeared as if the Yankees young budding superstar Joe DiMaggio had filled the gaping void resulting from a retired Babe Ruth. description_block: Offered here is one of the most coveted of all Honus Wagner baseball cards, his momentous 1910-11 M116 Sporting Life SGC EX-MT 4 marvel portraying the far scarcer blue background while boasting virtually perfect image positioning. One of a mere four SGC 4 copies at this highly coveted mid-grade tier, only six SGC examples have achieved a higher assessment. The M116 Sporting Life cards are amongst the most breathtaking subjects extant, enhanced by their stunning palette of pastel and blue colors. In 1910, the year after the “Flying Dutchman” led Pittsburgh to his first and only World Championship, these cards were first offered to subscribers of the Sporting Life periodical in 24 separate series of 12 cards each. Most of the portrait images are replicas of the classic Carl Horner photographs including the offered specimen of the immortal Hans Wagner. Over 300 subjects exist, with a small number depicting both blue and pastel backgrounds. It is no secret that the blue background subjects boast a much higher paucity level than their pastel brethren, with SGC listing 72 pastel Wagners versus only 29 blue examples (at the time this was written). The unconscionable rise of the pricing points for the “Holy Grail” T206 Wagner has been considerably infectious regarding its impact on the likewise surging values for other Honus Wagner cards portraying Carl Horner’s timeless portrait pose. Since an abundance of vintage collectors can ill afford the staggering $3+ million values for even “Authentic” T206 Wagner examples, they have deferred to other issues reflecting this classic Honus image. While pricing for these alternate Wagner “portrait pose” subjects was suppressed for the longest time, the past few years have seen a spiraling uptick for their still undervalued potential. Several examples of this pricing phenomena are Tip Top Bread Wagner cards in 2 – 4 grades fetching $125-$200K and M116 “Blue Background” mid-grade copies nailing down $72K (SGC 5.5) and $75K (PSA 5). Indeed, the floodgates have officially opened for the unlimited values of any portrait Wagner issue, and this eye-popping SGC 4 “Blue Background” offering certainly falls right into this prestigious category. The iconic Hans Wagner pose initially struck by Carl Horner at the turn of the 20th century resides as the cornerstone image of our illustrious hobby. No wonder passionate enthusiasts scramble to capture any cardboard issue portraying this immortal illustration that transcends time to an era when the great Wagner had established himself as our National Pastimes greatest all-time shortstop. With that in mind, what better card could one hope to obtain that one exhibiting an image tantamount with the “Holy Grail” T206 Wagner. One glance at this museum worthy memento can literally send chills through your spine, with the stoic Honus portrait pose exhibiting extremely rich pinkish facial hues and exceptional clarity. Elevating the classic illustration to a stratospheric level is the sparkling blue and green setting, with the time-defying image atypically boasting near-perfect centering between four bright white borders. This practically impossible to find feature places this grand keepsake at a pinnacle level, with most of its existing brethren plagued by severely skewed images. No notable creasing is evident, and the assessment is primarily due to even corner wear revealing an eye pleasing uniformity.  Along the lower edge is the bold black “Hans Wagner, Pitts. Nationals” text, and both sides have miraculously eluded any glaring flaws over the past 116 years. The final exclamation point is a bold midnight blue “SPORTING LIFE” advertisement proudly stating: “FOR 27 YEARS, THE RECOGNIZED AUTHROITY ON ALL BASEBALL MATTERS”, as well as listing its 5 Cents price to all newsdealers. For full disclosure, there appears to be an extremely faint horizontal pencil mark on the verso, extending from the right edge directly beneath the “FE” in “LIFE.” Barely visible, it is rendered virtually irrelevant versus the “heart-stopping” eye appeal of this magnificent rendering of the immortal “Flying Dutchman.”  One of the most captivating of all Wagner issues portraying his hallowed Carl Horner portrait image, it has stubbornly defied father-time”, proudly boasting his most sanctified image via a mesmerizing 50/50 state!

description_block: The continuous pricing spikes for the great Honus Wagner’s vintage cards is synonymous to a roaring tsunami, most likely prompted by his “Holy Grail” T206 subject as well as other previously undervalued Wagner mainstream issues finally receiving their due respect. This infectious inflation has spread to all of Han’s pre-WWI cards, with collectors frantically pursuing any of his esteemed keepsakes. That said, Goldin Auctions is proud to present one of the “Flying Dutchman’s” most elusive pre-WWI subjects, a PSA 2 GD 1911 D304 Weber Bakery offering that joins a mere four other copies on the illustrious PSA “Pop” Chart. Only two PSA examples have managed to surpass this exalted bread card (a “VG-EX+ 4.5” and “GD+ 2.5), with this ultra-elusive offering one of the rarest of all Honus Wagner collectibles and a fraction of the approximate 60+ known T206 Wagner’s. From 1911 through 1914, the Buffalo based General Bakery Company issued a 25-player baseball card set including five different advertisement backs to promote their popular bread products. Vintage collectors surely realize the immense paucity level of a Weber Bakery D304 subject versus the more plentiful Brunner’s Bread ad-backs. The set’s two rarest ad backs are Weber and Martens Bakery, with only 19 PSA encapsulated subjects boasting the extremely scarce Weber advertisement. Consider that of the total 565 D304 cards (for all 25 subjects) listed on the PSA census report at the time this was written, those 19 Weber Bakery specimens account for a meager 3.4% of the total population! There are 25 Martens subjects (4.4%); General Baking backs total 41 (7.3%), and Butter Krust includes 80 copies (14.2%), with the remaining ad backs revealing the common Brunners advertisement (Note, SGC population counts have been excluded from this exercise due to the significant number of crossovers from SGC to PSA, skewing the overall census numbers). Indeed, locating any Weber Bakery subject is an excruciating task, let alone one portraying the hallowed image of the incomparable Johannes Peter “Honus” Wagner. Along with his exalted T206 masterpiece, Wagner’s esteemed stature is certainly fueled by his unequivocal standing as baseball’s greatest all-time shortstop. A 1936 Hall of Fame Charter Member, Honus accumulated 3,418 lifetime hits to the tune of a sensational .328 batting average while stealing a lofty 723 bases. Wagner captured an N.L. record eight batting titles (tied with the great Tony Gwynn), with his .334 mark in 1911 good enough to claim his eighth and final batting championship. Most significantly, this museum worthy card’s verso boasts the obscure Weber Bakery advertisement, reading from top to bottom: “Compliments of WEBER BAKERY – General Baking Company – WRAPPED IN Butter = Nut AND Little General BREAD – NEWARK’S FAVORITES.”  Aside from some typical toning, no obtrusive defects are evident. The obverse side reveals the classic Wagner batting pose remarkably portraying near-perfect centering, with most of the D304 Wagner’s plagued by skewed images. The only notable crease is situated near the lower right corner, with the central image exhibiting extremely bright blue and green hues as well as reflecting superb clarity – immediately conjuring up vivid memories of the iconic baseball adage “blue sky; green grass.” The only notable blemishes are two somewhat modest horizontal and vertical soiling lines extending from all four borders while crossing each other directly above Wagner’s period-style belt. Possibly the result of prior rubber band usage, fortunately they do not extend onto the flipside, certainly not compromising the overall integrity of this super scarce bread card that proudly earned a “Top 30%” PWCC certification. The extraordinary $81K sale of a PSA 2 D304 Butter Krust Wagner earlier this year sent shockwaves throughout the collecting community, justifying the unlimited future prosperity for the great “Flying Dutchman’s” rarest D304 subjects!

card_name: Cy Young Signed June 12, 1939 First Day Cooperstown Cover
condition_note: Bold blue ink signature with approximate '9' strength.
special_note: Historical significance as it commemorates the inaugural induction ceremony of the Hall of Fame.
description_block: One of the memorabilia circuit’s most fascinating keepsakes is a June 12, 1939 First Day Cooperstown Cover signed by an illustrious Hall of Famer. Presented here is one of those highly coveted artifacts, boldly scripted in blue fountain pen by the immortal Cy Young! Truly one of our National Pastime’s most historical events was when the Hall of Fame first opened its doors for their inaugural induction ceremony on June 12, 1939 to commemorate not only baseball’s 100-year centennial, but to honor the 26 HOF inductees and five original 1936 HOF members. Some 12,000 passionate fans would show up, with the 26 electees from three different classes honored via bronze plaques that would forever grace the walls of this esteemed building. Numerous first-day mailing envelopes were issued for that momentous event by Postmaster General James A. Farley. Each included the postal June 12, 1939 date, “FIRST DAY OF ISSUE” postal stamps, and in this case, a line drawing of a batter completing his swing as well as a baseball diamond including the caption: “BASEBALL CENTENNIEL 1839-1939.”  Somewhat unique, this revered offering includes several imposing descriptions relating to the great Cy Young’s unparallelled excellence, reading as follows: “THIS RECORD WITHOUT ANY DOUBT WILL BE THE HARDEST TO EVER BE BROKEN IN BASEBALL” as well as “CY YOUNG – THE GREATEST BASEBALL PITCHER OF ALL TIME WHO WON 511 GAMES AND LOST 313 FOR PERCENTAGE OF .620 DURING HIS 22 YEARS IN MAJOR LEAGUES.  AUTOGRPAHED BY HIM ON JUNE 12TH 1939, OUT OF COOPERSTOWN NEW YORK.”  Apropos to say the least, no MLB pitcher will ever remotely approach 511 wins, with this resounding benchmark baseball’s most unbreakable record. It therefore came as little surprise when the annual award for pitching excellence was named after the iconic Cy Young, and his bold blue ink horizontal signature revealing approximate “9” strength is a perfect testament for his arguable legacy as the “best of the best!”

description_block:
The electrifying 2019 "Uncle Jimmy Collection" find that produced a vast number of signed Babe Ruth Goudey cards sent a resounding message throughout the hobby regarding the undervalued status of a signed Babe Ruth Goudey card. At that time, scripted Goudey Ruth's were selling at a fraction of their true prospective value, with a #181 signed Goudey Ruth recently fetching a record $1.5 million in Goldin's February Vintage Auction! This landmark sale substantiated the potential stratospheric pricing points for a signed Babe Ruth Goudey, and based on the lofty $7 million-plus price tags currently associated with a multitude of signed modern day cards, autographed 1933 Goudey Ruth subjects still haven't even touched the "tip of the iceberg" regarding their future prosperity. That said, presented here just happens to be another one of those coveted scripted Babe Ruth Goudey's, a splendid PSA VG 3 (MC) 1933 Goudey #144 marvel boasting a bold PSA/DNA NM 7 "Babe Ruth" autograph (30098559). At the time this was written, this POP 1 heirloom was only bested by a paltry three PSA copies (qualifiers notwithstanding), with only nine #144 examples listed on the prestigious PSA/DNA "Pop" Chart in any grade. Joining the aforementioned $1.5 million sale of a signed #181 subject are other immense sales for autographed Ruth Goudey's including $1.2 million for a #149 PSA 4/Auto 8 subject (2025 private sale); a recent $1.3 million for a #53 PSA 3.5/Auto 8 specimen (2026 private sale), and nearly $600,000 for an inferior #144 PSA 2/Auto 7 copy in 2025. These spiraling prices justify that the floodgates have surely opened regarding the stratospheric-like values for a signed Goudey Ruth, and as the most meticulous collector can surely see, there is seemingly no end in sight for this tsunami-like pricing surge.
Captivating to say the least, the prospect of owning a Babe Ruth signed Goudey bubble gum card immediately provides its fortunate new owner unparalleled bragging rights for years to come. The sheer notion of capturing any such artifact is the passionate driving force for numerous elite hobbyists, especially when that rarity is associated with the incomparable George Herman "Babe" Ruth. It would make perfect sense for any of these previously undervalued signed Babe Ruth Goudey cards to finally "hit their stride," especially considering modern signed cards such as a LeBron James rookie and the recent Michael Jordan/Kobe Bryant signed card have recorded remarkable $5.2 million and $12.9 million sales, respectively, with the $12.9 million price a record for any sports card. Adding to this unrestrained pricing uptick was the unconscionable $16.5 million sale of a Pokémon POP 1 PSA 10 Illustrator card earlier this year in a Goldin Auction. A bona fide record sale for ANY trading card, while the card was not autographed, its miraculous pricing point makes a resounding statement to the collecting community—sports or non-sports—that there are no restrictions regarding the boundless limits for the value of an extremely popular trading card. Therefore, one must truly consider the possible infinite-like value of a highly coveted signed Ruth Goudey marvel; representing the undisputed greatest all-time player who ever graced a baseball diamond! Indeed, this grand offering resides as the perfect testament for the "Sultan of Swat" who via his colossal home runs, remarkable batting achievements, including out-homering virtually every MLB team in the early 1920s, and unmatched personality will forever stand as our National Pastime's "best of the best." Issued in 1933 by the Goudey Gum Co. of Boston, Massachusetts, this "heart-stopping" gem was originally part of a landmark 240-subject set featuring a host of Cooperstown Inductees including four different Ruth cards. The prior 1932 campaign saw the mighty Bambino lead his Yankees to a four-game sweep of the Chicago Cubs in the Fall Classic. The highlight of this series would be Ruth's iconic "Called Shot" home run in the fifth inning of Game #3 at Wrigley Field, when "the Babe" allegedly pointed to centerfield before an 0-2 pitch and then blasted a Charlie Root fastball off of the Cubs scoreboard for what is still considered the longest dinger ever walloped at Wrigley Field. Who could possibly contest why the prestigious Goudey Gum Company chose Ruth to appear on four different Goudey cards (Nos. 53, 144, 149, 181), for entering the 1933 season, Ruth had already blasted 652 home runs–eventually ending his unparalleled 22-year career with a resounding 714 lifetime dingers.
This majestic Ruthian offering surely merits a final resting place in the most esteemed autograph or Babe Ruth gathering. The presentation is highlighted by the iconic Charles Conlon full Babe Ruth batting pose, originally taken in 1927 by this legendary photographer and one of baseball's foremost classic Bambino poses. It is clearly obvious the overall aesthetics of the central image are more consistent with a mid-grade example via its host of sparkling red, green and yellow hues, relatively strong corners as well as its superb resolution. Preventing a higher assessment is a light diagonal mark situated directly above Ruth's hands and running along the bat through his period-style Yankees cap. Most significantly, this defect does not compromise the immortal "Babe Ruth" black fountain pen signature affixed across his pinstriped pantaloons, arguably revealing "8" strength (versus the rather harsh PSA 7 assessment). For full disclosure, the "MC" mis-cut qualifier is due to the card being factory issued with a minimal right border, yet as most enthusiasts would agree, the coupled outstanding central image aesthetics and Cooperstown worthy autograph take front and center stage, clearly "stealing the show" as a momentous dynamic duo. No severe creasing or other unsightly imperfections are evident on either side, with a clean verso the final exclamation point. If you are assembling some of Ruth's most formidable, signed artifacts, this may be your final opportunity to capture one of his finest available mementos. All signed Goudey Babe Ruth subjects suffice as quintessential marketing tools for the economic 101 philosophy—"today's retail is tomorrow's wholesale." As previously stated, the "signed sports-card" market is currently achieving a myriad of record-breaking prices, and we cannot imagine a more imposing scripted card than any of the four Goudey Ruth subjects. When you consider Babe Ruth's incomparable standing in baseball history as both a stellar pitcher for the Boston Red Sox and outstanding New York Yankees slugger, his overall stature cannot be overemphasized. The "Sultan of Swat's" sheer existence stands above the game itself, so it should come as little surprise that his signed cards are finally receiving the recognition they justly deserve, evident by the most recent autographed Goudey Ruth lucrative sales. This esteemed artifact provides a golden opportunity to claim one of the most revered of all Babe Ruth collectibles. The rarest and most highly-coveted sports cards are now viewed as not only collectibles, but as legitimate investment commodities. That said, the next Babe Ruth "Queen Mary" heirloom has officially pulled into port and considering the previous $1.5 million sale of a signed Goudey Ruth earlier this year, we will defer to the sophisticated collector to ultimately determine the true worth of this likewise exalted #144 Goudey Babe Ruth autographed prize!

description_block: This splendid carte de visite was produced by a self-proclaimed—and demonstrably talented—"Photographic Artist" in the Boston, Mass. region within the few years following the end of the American Civil War. The squad is pictured in a serious, properly posed group consisting of nine fully uniformed players and two civilian-attired businessmen who likely served as managers or executives. The albumen picture is adhered to a thick-cardboard mount, in standard cdv fashion, measuring approximately 2-1/2-by-4-inches. The reverse side of the mount carries two bits of information—"W.H. Getchell, (Of the late firm of Case & Getchell)" and "375 Washington Street, Boston. Next Door South of Adams House."—separated by the "Photographic Artist" credit stamp in bold Gothic lettering. Upon investigation, it can be quickly discovered that while Mr. Getchell practiced his calling for several decades, he only did so at the "South of Adams ..." location from 1866 to 1872. It has been speculated that the featured athletes and support personnel were associated with a "Lowell Base Ball Club," a term that did identify one prominent squad of the day but which has since become somewhat of a catch-all descriptor for the various local teams that proliferated in Massachusetts during the sport's postbellum formative years. These men and their club's specific identities, though, have stubbornly eluded precise, modern-day assignment. The members' surviving likenesses, however, are distinguished by remarkably crisp integrity, and the artifact delivering their team portrayal concedes only minor traces of past handling. So, although the gentlemen featured in this depiction might not have directly faced off to claim the New England area's coveted Silver Ball Trophy, and were thus deprived of that measure of notoriety, their competitive spirits have nonetheless achieved immortality in this sublime antique's spellbinding image.

condition_note: Corners display expected degrees of rounding from past handling; small crease at bottom-right corner.
special_note: Highly sought after and one of the most valuable vintage football cards.
description_block: Graded GD 2 by PSA (63426693). Hall of Famer, in his justifiably prized Rookie Card appearance. Here is the undisputed key card from the foundation issue of the football collecting hobby. The 1935 National Chicle Bronko Nagurski entry represents, by far, the single most valuable and avidly pursued subject among the realm of vintage football cards. A true one-of-a-kind, larger-than-life figure, Minnesota native and eventual Canton enshrinee starred for the Chicago Bears and was one of the earliest, universally acclaimed superstars of his sport. In this spellbinding paper heirloom, evocative cardback text—highlighting a detail that couldn't apply to any other gridiron combatant within living memory—summarizes, "He is one of the few players versatile enough to play any position on the team without losing his effectiveness." Nagurski became a standout playing both tackle on defense and fullback on offense at the University of Minnesota (1927-1929). He was selected as a consensus All-American in 1929 and inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame in its inaugural year of 1951. His professional career with the Chicago Bears, which began in 1930 and ended on two occasions in 1937 and 1943, was distinguished by three NFL Championships and four First-team All-Pro nods. Nagurski's uniquely impressive résumé and, certainly, his reputation, also compelled his timely selection as an inaugural inductee into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1963. Further evidence of this peerless competitor's versatility: during his pro football career, Nagurski built a second, well-earned identity as a professional wrestler, and in that punishing arena, too, he became a major box-office attraction. (Nagurski's wrestling activities continued until the late 1950s.) Nagurski's—essentially, mandatory!—inclusion in the first meaningful trading card production to feature professional gridiron stars was only natural, and he completed the legitimization of the beautiful, artistically conceived series with his presence. His elusive card, number 34, is situated within the extremely scarce "high number" segment of the issue. This card is very difficult to obtain under any circumstances, and examples boasting favorable aesthetic qualities are especially tough to find. The offered card is particularly noteworthy for its striking colors and vivid printing. The piece has been spared much of the toning from age that affects so many classics from the 1930s (with just a few small, transparent areas revealing any difference in hue), and the item presents with enviable freshness. The corners display expected degrees of rounding from past handling, but Nagurski's image is nicely focused, and the card is quite clean, front and back. The portrayal concedes a small crease at the bottom-right corner, but this liability poses minimal disturbance in terms of eye appeal. The inevitably well-informed and responsive, modern-day hobby market readily acknowledges the enduring importance of this special collectible. Another PSA GD 2 example changed hands for nearly $37,000 in a major auction house's October 2025 sale. More recently, an estimable PSA VG 3 copy fetched just shy of $50,000 in a January 2026 event while a PSA 5 example nailed down a staggering $119K only two months ago. Here, then is a highly worthy, immensely enticing specimen of what can easily be characterized as one of the world's most desirable football cards, and it stands as a piece that will measurably enhance the stature of an advanced collection or thoughtfully curated portfolio.
