description_block:
The highly coveted 1955 Topps Roberto Clemente Rookie is presented here in a sparkling PSA 8 NM-MT holder, with only 15 specimens or 0.2% of the approximate 7,700 encapsulated examples managing to exceed this magnificent offering! It is no secret that extremely high-end rookie cards continue to achieve staggering values, with one “MINT 9” Clemente fetching an extraordinary $1.1 million in the Spring of 2021, and a PSA 8 pushing the $160K mark only some six months ago. However, what makes this unfathomable offering extra special is both the MBA Silver Diamond Certification and its near-perfect centering. An unparalleled “one-two” punch, most Clemente rookies are plagued by unsightly image positioning and both the pack-fresh surfaces and extraordinary centering more than justify the critical MBA sticker. It is surely no secret that vintage cards boasting any MBA certification level are currently experiencing lofty pricing upticks, with a bona fide example of this value phenomenon being a PSA 9 MBA Certified 1956 Topps Mickey Mantle fetching $414K in an October 2025 public auction – a roughly 175% spike over its typical $140-$160K value. The coupled PSA 8 assessment and Roberto’s world-class accomplishments certainly substantiate why advanced hobbyists painstakingly pursue one of his spectacular high grade rookie cards. Some of Clemente’s magnificent accolades include a .317 lifetime batting average, 3,000 career hits, the 1966 regular season MVP award, four batting titles, 12 consecutive gold glove awards, and if that isn’t enough, a 1971 World Series MVP when he dominated the Baltimore Orioles via his stellar hitting and fielding prowess. Yet, he will always be best remembered for his tragic death when, after the 1972 season, his plane crashed carrying supplies to assist earthquake victims in Nicaragua – with the “Steel City” superstar now belonging to the ages. 
The iconic right fielder commenced his professional baseball career in October 1952 when he signed his first pro-contract with the renowned Cangrejeros de Santurce Puerto Rican Winter League club (playing in only several games and batting an unimpressive .234). The next season, Clemente would be given a starting job in the outfield, posting a .288 average and catching the eye of many professional scouts via his exceptional five-tool skill sets. While he would continue playing for this prominent Winter League club, the Dodgers signed him in the amateur draft in February 1954, assigning him to play with the celebrated Montreal Royals. After a single season with Montreal, the Pirates would eventually select Clemente in the rookie draft, signing the star right-fielder on November 22, 1954. Clemente would capture a championship with the 1954/'55 Cangrejeros club, and made his MLB debut on April 17, 1955, posting his first MLB hit in a 10-3 Pirates loss to the Brooklyn Dodgers at Forbes Field. Although his rookie season would see the future Cooperstown inductee bat only .255 on a last-place club, his laundry list of electrifying skill sets including amazing bat control, a powerful throwing arm, sensational fielding prowess and superb base running captivated the Pittsburgh faithful. No wonder the illustrious Topps Chewing Gum Co. decided to include Clemente in their renowned 1955 set as the sanctified #164 subject, with this 71 year-old keepsake joining the 1951 Bowman Mantle and Mays inaugural subjects as one of the three most valuable post-WWII “vintage” rookie cards extant.  
Like Clemente’s uncanny playing superiority is this remarkable offering that appears as if it has just been pulled from a 1955 wax pack from a local “mom & pop” store. A gleaming surface includes legendary portrait and batting poses, both exhibiting vivid resolution and an extensive array of brilliant hues. As previously stated, the highlight is the virtually 50/50 image positioning, neatly situated between four snow white borders that lead to blistering sharp edging. Indeed, there are no “rough” factory cut edges, with the four right-angled corners and near-immaculate surfaces additional “heart-stopping” features. The final superlative is a relatively clean verso; likewise revealing excellent centering. This extremely well-preserved rookie card is a perfect testament for Clemente’s incomparable stature that will forever stand the test of time. Most would agree the HOF right fielder represented the embodiment of human valor, well demonstrated via his courageous actions that would tragically claim his life the final day of 1972 to assist stricken individuals. A literal “superman” both on and off the field, we cannot imagine a finer dynamic duo than a high-grade Roberto Clemente rookie card complimented by the momentous MBA Silver Certification, leaving an enamored number of meticulous collectors to ultimately decide its true worth!

description_block: Locating a 1967 Topps Tom Seaver rookie card portraying near “dead-on” 50/50 centering is an excruciating task, justifying why this miraculous PSA 9 Mint ’67 Topps “Tom Terrific” inaugural keepsake boasting near-perfect image positioning is one of the finest known copies extant. Bested by only a meager three PSA 10 examples, its pinnacle-like stature is consistent with Seaver’s solidified place as one of baseball’s ten greatest all-time pitchers. His immediate success prompted the Topps Chewing Gum Company to incorporate Seaver as their #581 subject along with long-forgotten Bill Denehy in the scarcer “high-numbered” final series. Seaver’s true 1967 rookie card was officially born, now residing as one of the most iconic post-WWII inaugural HOF issues. Soon to be dubbed “The Franchise”, Tom Seaver was an unquestionable “winner”, and two years later, his 25 wins and first of three Cy Young awards would lead the “Miracle Mets” to their first championship. The HOF right-hander would end his remarkable 20-year career with 311 wins, 3,640 strikeouts and a miraculous 2.86 lifetime E.R.A., standing alongside Walter Johnson as one of only two MLB pitchers who compiled 300+ wins, 3,000+ strikeouts and a sub-3.00 E.R.A. Additional worldly feats include striking out a record 10 consecutive batters (19 in all) on April 22, 1970 against San Diego (tied by two pitchers in 2021), and he is still the only pitcher in baseball history to fan 200 or more batters in nine consecutive seasons. He tossed 61 shutouts, 231 complete games twenty-seven 3-hitters, ten 2-hitters, five one-hitters, and a no-hitter against St. Louis in his first season with Cincinnati. Unfathomable to say the least, Seaver yielded two earned runs or less in nearly 250 of his 311 lifetime wins, further justifying why many historians consider him as the arguable greatest post-WWII pitcher.  The card reveals all the pack-fresh attributes required for a “9” assessment including a spellbinding image, brilliant hues, blistering sharp corner tips, pristine-like surfaces, and of course, the previously mentioned near-perfect centering. It was the legendary Mark Twain who was once quoted: “the two most important days of our lives are the day we were born with the second being a clear understanding of why we were born? Regarding the immortal George Thomas Seaver, significant day number one was his November 17, 1944 birth date with his true destiny ultimately being to captivate an adoring Nation via his unparalleled skill set for throwing a baseball to a catcher with uncanny speed and control. Indeed, “The” Franchise” was the “best of the best”, and we cannot imagine a finer testament to his storied 20-year career than this immaculate PSA 9 rookie card issued the year Tom Terrific was about to embark on a career for the ages!

description_block:
The scarcity of the hobby’s "Holy Grail" T206 Honus Wagner does not even remotely match the rarity level of this incredibly elusive 1910 E104-2 Nadja Caramel Wagner SGC 4 keepsake, for which there are only eight documented copies in any grade! Boasting the same iconic Carl Horner portrait pose of baseball’s greatest all-time shortstop, this extraordinary offering stands alone at its SGC mid-grade assessment on the combined PSA and SGC census reports, with a meager two SGC 5 examples graded higher! Furthermore, its unparalleled paucity level only reveals five other lower graded examples, substantiating that its sheer existence is a mere fraction of the highly celebrated T206 Wagner for which there are approximately 60 known specimens. Indeed, the E104-2 Wagner subject’s "pop" is approximately 13% of its T206 Wagner brethren, and it is easier to find a needle in a haystack than come across one of the "Flying Dutchman’s" Nadja issues. Its irrefutable obscurity places it as a far scarcer issue than other Honus issues as well, including his 1903-11 W600 Type 3 & 4 Sporting Life Cabinets, 1910 E103 Williams Caramel, 1910 D322 Tip Top Bread, 1910 E90-2 American Caramel, and 1911 M116 Sporting Life subjects—all of which portray Horner’s classic Hans portrait image. Therefore, it came as little surprise that a low-grade SGC 1.5 FR E104-2 Wagner recently fetched a whopping $81,000 in Goldin’s February Vintage Auction, and we cannot even begin to estimate what one of the finest copies such as this compelling SGC 4 marvel is truly worth. The 1910 Nadja Caramel 14-subject set was regionally distributed in the "Steel City" to commemorate the Pirates’ 1909 World Series victory, with Wagner’s fourth consecutive batting title via an outstanding .339 mark paving the way for Pittsburgh’s inaugural championship. The immortal "Flying Dutchman" totally outplayed the great Ty Cobb in their first and only head-to-head matchup en route to Pittsburgh’s exhilarating victory in a tightly contested seven games. One of Wagner’s rarest cards, this offering includes a blank verso, and to the best of our knowledge, all of the other documented seven examples likewise reveal a blank verso. The T206 Honus Wagner will forever reside as the hobby’s "Holy Grail," and while every cardboard collector fantasizes about owning this card, low-grade specimens now require $5 million budgets (a PSA 1 copy just realized $5.1 million in Goldin’s February Vintage Auction, with an "Authentic" copy nailing down $3.6 million). Capturing a T206 Wagner has evolved into a near-impossible financial conquest, substantiating why recent prices for similar pre-WWI Wagner issues portraying the same legendary Wagner portrait illustration are also surging in value tantamount to a raging tsunami. Undervalued for the longest time, the floodgates have opened with regard to soaring price tags. Over the past two to three years, several Tip Top Wagners have fetched $156,000 (3-VG) and $137,000 (2-GOOD), two M116 blue background Wagners nailed down $75,000 (5 EX) and $52,000 (3-VG), with a few E90-2 copies realizing $117,000 (EX 5) and $111,000 (VG-EX 4). There certainly appears to be no end in sight for these immense pricing upticks, with this E104-2 Nadja Wagner proudly standing tall as one of his most miraculous cardboard collectibles. Boasting a fractional existence versus its T206 Wagner brethren, its incomparable rarity, immortal Carl Horner lithographic Wagner pose, and outstanding aesthetics all combine to formulate a resounding "trifecta."
Similar to a host of other early 20th century candy "E" cards, E104-2 subjects exhibit extreme condition sensitivity, with this time withstanding, 116-year-old marvel defying logic via its spectacular eye appeal and near-impossible to find mid-grade assessment. Of utmost significance, the relatively well-positioned legendary Wagner pose is eye-popping to say the least, depicting only a forgiving partiality toward the right edge. Most significantly, the classic central pose boasts sparkling facial hues including robust rosy cheeks, exceptional clarity, and a super bold blue background. Tantamount to the handful of other known examples, there are a few light horizontal print lines situated in the upper region, all factory-issued and rendered virtually irrelevant versus the card’s sheer existence and regal beauty. For full disclosure, the upper and lower borders reflect a commonly seen "butterfly" (angled) factory cut, and the borders show even toning. Accounting for the grade is even corner wear, with each corner revealing some subtle etching near their outermost perimeters. The final exclamation point is a super clean blank back, and most would agree that the iconic Carl Horner central pose on this grand copy arguably qualifies as the finest of the eight known examples. To reiterate, the combined PSA/SGC "Pop" charts list only eight total E104-2 Wagners versus some 60 known examples of the T206 "Holy Grail," with an SGC 2 T206 Wagner fetching a staggering $7.25 million in a 2023 private sale, and a PSA 1 realizing $5.1 million earlier this year. It is clearly obvious that any of the previously mentioned portrait Wagner subjects are immensely undervalued versus the megamillion-dollar price tags associated with its T206 peer. Now consider that this exalted Nadja heirloom reflects only eight documented graded specimens, representing a fractional 13% of the T206 Wagner population. The future prosperity of the T206 Wagner is a "sure thing," and likewise, its strikingly similar portrait counterparts may not have even touched the "tip of the iceberg" regarding their unlimited investment potential. Equally impressive is the unwavering presence of any Wagner portrait subject standing tall as a cornerstone of America’s favorite pastime, effectively transcending the avid fan back in time when the immortal Pirates shortstop was embarking on a career eventually placing him as one of baseball’s five original 1936 HOF charter members. One glance at this Cooperstown-worthy heirloom immediately conjures up majestic memories of DeWolf Hopper’s "Casey at the Bat" and Jack Norworth’s "Take Me Out to the Ballgame," as well as rekindling thoughts of America’s "Star Spangled Banner" national anthem; Ty Cobb violently sliding into third base with his spikes flying high, the mighty Bambino walloping another majestic home run into the grandstands, or simply a captivated youth scrambling to their local "mom & pop" store to open a pack of baseball cards. Truly, this momentous Honus candy card treat prompts all these charismatic visions, turning back the clock to an era when Johannes Peter "Honus" Wagner was establishing himself as our national pastime’s greatest all-time shortstop. The unparalleled "swagger" of the hallowed E104-2 Nadja Caramel Honus portrait pose cannot be overemphasized, with its unequivocal rarity and T206 likeness a resounding "dynamic duo" forever etched in the hearts of the most passionate collectors!

description_block: Presented here is one of Joe DiMaggio’s scarcest early playing days issues, his obscure 1937 V300 O-Pee-Chee Die-Cut PSA 3 memento. Fresh to the hobby, this offering is part of a recent vintage card discovery, and advanced collectors are well aware of the painstaking task for capturing this "Joltin’ Joe" rarity. At the time this was written, PSA had only encapsulated 37 DiMaggio’s in any grade, less than three copies of the likewise scarce 1936 WWG DiMaggio rookie card for which there are 40 examples. One of the most elusive of all pre-WWII cardboard issues is the seldom surfacing 1937 O-Pee-Chee die-cuts. Designated as V300 by the American Card Catalog, the 1937 O-Pee-Chee "die-cuts" measure approximately 2-5/8" x 2-15/16" and appear to be a combination of the '34 Goudey and 1934-36 Batter-Up sets, as well as including some similar images later utilized on the 1940-41 Play Ball subjects. Printed in black & white, player images were die-cut approximately near the center of the card in order that the top portion could be folded back to create a stand-up card. Along with the “true” Bob Feller rookie card, the set's most valuable and coveted subject is the iconic Hall of Fame centerfielder Joe DiMaggio, with the Yankee Clipper's '37 O-Pee-Chee his bona fide "second year” issue. No baseball player could possibly boast the popularity and admiration bestowed upon the legendary Yankee Clipper. Throughout his playing days and post-retirement years, “Joltin’ Joe's” overall persona was perceived with unequivocal respect, as he represented the ultimate embodiment of a national hero. His 56-game hitting streak in 1941 prompted an ultra-popular song, personifying everything he meant to the grand ole game. The exalted DiMaggio "batting" image depicts outstanding contrast and clarity, set against a relatively clean baseball diamond. While not the exact same image, this batting pose is strikingly similar to his 1936 R315 Rookie Premium as well as his 1940-41 Play Ball illustrations – all taken during a 1936 photo shoot by legendary baseball photographer Geroge Burke. No glaring defects are evident on either side, with general surface wear/toning and corner aging accounting for the grade. Truly, the overall aesthetics surpass the rather “stingy” technical assessment, and the final compliment is a relatively clean verso that reveals a brief DiMaggio “bio” in both English and French. Issued during the year this immortal Yankee would once again team up with Yankees Captain Lou Gehrig to lead the Brox Bombers to their second successive world championship, DiMaggio would pace the Junior Circuit with 46 homers and a robust .673 Slugging Percentage, while also posting a resounding .346 batting average and 167 R.B.I.’s. The Yankee Clipper was well on his way to becoming one of baseball’s greatest all-time players, and this immensely elusive 1937 O-Pee-Chee PSA 3 marvel proudly stands as a perfect testament for Joe’s early Yankees playing days!

description_block:
Cert #: 1P05413
Notes: A visually stunning and historically significant pre-war baseball image from the game’s formative era. Few photographers documented baseball’s Deadball Era with the artistry and historical importance of legendary lensman Charles Conlon.
This exceptional 4.25-by-6.5 inch image captures “Wee Willie” Keeler during the twilight of one of baseball’s most celebrated careers. The portrait possesses the exact visual power collectors seek in premier Conlon imagery — razor-sharp facial detail, dramatic tonal contrast, and the timeless intimacy that defined Conlon’s finest work.
Most notably, the image exhibits the unmistakable qualities of a National Baseball Hall of Fame plaque-style portrait, elevating its display appeal far beyond the typical period news photograph. Keeler’s intense expression and classic New York cap insignia combine to create an enduring visual representation of early professional baseball.
Immortalized for the phrase: “Hit ’em where they ain’t," Keller retired with as a two-time Batting Champion and a member of the legendary 3,000-hit-club, with a career .341 batting average. Keeler remains one of the foundational offensive stars of the Deadball Era, and was inducted into the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 1939.
About Original/Vintage Photos: This auction category may include studio photos, promo photos, press photos, news-service photos, card-used photos, team-issued photos, snapshot photos, etc. PSA/DNA is currently the leading authentication company in the photography space. The Photo Type Classification System© was created in the 2005 book A Portrait of Baseball Photography by co-authors Henry Yee, Marshall Fogel and Khyber Oser, and it has been licensed exclusively to PSA/DNA since 2007. Type I - Developed from the original negative within approximately 2 years of the picture being taken. Type II - Developed from the original negative more than approximately 2 years after the picture was taken. Type III - Developed from a duplicate negative, wire transmission or digital printing within approximately 2 years of the picture being taken. Type IV - Developed from a duplicate negative, wire transmission or digital printing more than approximately 2 years after the picture was taken. Goldin's Original/Vintage Photos may show evidence of usage and wear such as crop marks, editorial masking, handwritten notations, file stamps, paper captions, creasing, crazing, staining, foxing, chipping, edge tears, missing corners, etc. PSA's slabs/holders may also bear incidental streaks, marks and scratches. description_block: One of the “Splendid Splinter’s’ most celebrated cardboard keepsakes is his legendary 1941 Play Ball #14 subject, presented here in an outstanding PSA NM 7 holder. Truly residing as one of “Teddy Ballgame’s” most formidable baseball cards, hobbyists crave this issue most likely due to both the season it was issued as well as the super eye pleasing Williams’ portrait pose that is a bona fide collector favorite. Despite a batting average of .406 and leading the league in home runs (37), Ted Williams' career year in '41 still didn't yield an MVP Award for the Boston legend. (Williams also had the game-winning blast in the ninth inning of the 1941 All-Star Game to cement the American League's victory.) As it turned out, Joe DiMaggio's record-setting 56 consecutive game hitting streak ultimately pushed baseball writers in choosing the Yankee Clipper as the Junior Circuit’s MVP, but it didn't diminish the latter’s remarkable season. “The Kid’s” unparalleled hitting prowess has placed him as our National Pastime’s greatest all-time hitter, and it is not every time that we could fulfill our lifetime dream. Indeed, the great Bo-Sox slugger did achieve his ultimate goal of “walking down the street with people passing me and saying there goes the greatest hitter who ever lived.” This notion is substantiated by Ted’s .344 lifetime average, 521 home runs, nearly 2,000 R.B.I.’s and the second highest OPS (1.115) and OPS+ (190) figures that sit a close second to the immortal Babe Ruth. All these amazing achievements were compiled with Williams missing five years of his “prime” in WWII and the Korean War as a bona-fide fighter pilot, with Ted’s incomparable MLB career spanning four decades (1939-1960). Like “the Thumper’s” sensational batting exploits are the outstanding aesthetics of this well-preserved PSA 7 subject that has rightfully earned the hallowed assessment. Issued during the memorable 1941 campaign, it features a treasured likeness in an admirably bright and barely toned, hardly touched state of preservation. The card displays clean borders that surround a strong, well-focused image. Stealing the show is the near-perfect centering, a scarce accomplishment for an issue typically plagued by skewed illustrations. Preventing a higher assessment is subtle wear to the relatively square corners, and both sides have eluded any glaring imperfections. A resounding testament to Ted Williams’ unequivocal legacy, it conjures up vivid memories of how this magnificent hitter elevated himself to a pinnacle level at his gifted craft. The true embodiment of a national hero and the last player to achieve the exalted .400 mark, this Beantown icon electrified America’s favorite pastime for nearly 20 years, ironically synonymous with the captivating eye appeal emanating from this classic 1941 commemorative!

description_block:
One of the finest 1951 Bowman Mickey Mantle rookie cards you will ever encounter, its coupled PSA NM-MT 8 assessment and breathtaking aesthetics substantiate its iconic stature, certainly appearing as if was just inserted into a 1951 Bowman wax pack! Finding a superior graded specimen is an excruciating task, with PSA's illustrious "POP" chart only listing a fractional 10 of the nearly 2,900 total encapsulated copies at a higher grade. The 1951 Bowman and 1952 Topps Mickey Mantle subjects indisputably stand as two of the foremost sports cards extant, both tied to the "Commerce Comet's" early MLB origin. Justifying that notion is the record-setting $12.6 million sale of an SGC 9.5 MT+ 1952 Topps Mickey Mantle in August 2022 that sent shockwaves throughout the hobby, the highest amount ever paid for a publicly sold pre-2000 vintage sports card. While the 1952 Topps #311 Mantle does suffice as the post-WWII's undisputed "Holy Grail," it is certainly not "the Mick's" true rookie card. That unique distinction belongs to the highly celebrated 1951 Bowman #253 subject, and it was only some four years ago that a PSA 9 Mantle rookie realized a record setting $3.2 million. Indeed, the future prosperity of high-grade copies appears to have no limitations, with two PSA 8 specimens fetching a whopping $615K in 2021. While not a "MINT 9" example, this offering's outstanding visual appeal has likewise defied father-time over the past 75 years, impressively boasting many of its factory issued attributes. Undervalued for the longest time versus its 1952 Topps Mantle brethren, pack-fresh examples of the "Commerce Comet's" 1951 Bowman subject retain unlimited investment potential since it proudly represents Mantle's bona fide inaugural card. One of the foremost aspects of the 1951 Bowman Mantle rookie card is the fact that he is showcasing his initial #6 Yankees road flannels, some four months before he would eventually swap #6 for his iconic #7 jersey. The Spring of 1951 would be an exciting time in the "Big Apple" for it marked the introduction of both Mickey Mantle and Willie Mays to the Gotham state. The ultra-powerful Mickey Charles Mantle displayed supernatural-like batting exploits, making his renowned MLB Yankee debut on April 17, 1951 while donning #6 on his pinstriped uniform. Playing in front of 44,860 patrons at Yankee Stadium, Mantle would earn his inaugural major league hit, while knocking in and scoring a run in the Yankees 5-0 win against their arch-rival Red Sox. This incredibly strong switch-hitter was the talk of the town, and although he had to start his highly anticipated career in right field due to "Joltin'" Joe DiMaggio still patrolling centerfield, his uncanny batting prowess and Secretariat-like speed created an unprecedented excitement amongst the New York faithful. Unfortunately for this rookie sensation, he eventually wallowed in a horrible slump, striking out a prolific number of times leading to his July 14 demotion to the Yankees AAA Kansas City squad (after a dismal July 13 1-5 performance in which he struck out three times). His self-esteem totally shattered, Mickey had endured all he could possibly handle and was ready to "throw in the towel" and call it quits. At that juncture, his father Mutt Mantle came to get his bewildered son who was expecting dad to lovingly embrace and console him. Certainly not the case because Mutt called him a coward and was ready to drag him back to the Oklahoma coal mines. It was that sheer motivation that pushed Mantle forward, dry his eyes and pack his bags for Kansas City. The rest of the story is history with Mickey burying his fears and literally tearing up AAA to the tune of a .361 batting average and 11 round-trippers. HOF manager Casey Stengel pushed the Yankee front office to re-call Mantle to the big leagues on August 24, with Mickey now wearing his #7 uniform for the first time. Playing against the Cleveland Indians at Municipal Stadium, Mantle would go 1-4 in New York's 2-0 win against the Tribe. Fortunately for collectors, the prestigious Bowman Gum Co. had already released his #253 subject revealing the immortal Mick in his original #6 uniform, with the "Oklahoma Kid's" legendary card now belonging to the ages.
Interesting enough, the undervalued status of a PSA 8 Bowman Mantle rookie versus his 1952 Topps subject is clearly substantiated by the pricing points for each versus their PSA population counts. At the time this was written, there were 53 PSA 8 1951 Bowman Mantles versus 35 1952 Topps #311 subjects—a 50 percent census advantage for the 1951 Bowman example. However, PSA 8 NM-MT '52 Topps Mantle’s consistently fetch seven-figures-plus (a stunning 100 percent to 400 percent advantage) versus the roughly $400K to $600K pricing points for a PSA 8 Mantle rookie! This mystifying pricing disparity certainly supports the notion that a high-grade 1951 Bowman Mantle is significantly undervalued, boasting unlimited investment potential. Indeed, tantamount to one of "the Mick's" tape-measure home runs that could test the confines of even Yellowstone Park, his 1951 Bowman rookie card truly knows no bounds. However the Mickey Mantle mystique was established, no one will argue that Mantle's 1951 Bowman image will forever be embedded in hobby lore, and along with the 1952 Topps Mantle, is one of the few post-war cards rightfully standing alongside the T206 Honus Wagner "Holy Grail" regarding their unequivocal stature. Mantle was Goliath, Davey Crockett, John Wayne and Joe DiMaggio all rolled up into one super icon, the fundamental embodiment of a national hero. Indeed, what card could better represent the strength of our hobby than one of Mantle's well-preserved inaugural cardboard issues, with this PSA 8 cardboard treasure featuring a myriad of qualities consistent with an example just pulled from a 1951 Bowman wax pack at a local "mom and pop" store. Some of its compelling features include impeccable clarity, a brilliant host of gray/blue hues, immaculate-like surfaces, dazzling white borders, and the complete absence of any unsightly vertical print lines. The classic "bat over shoulder" lithographic pose, portraying Mickey's hallowed #6 inaugural uniform, was utilized from a classic 1951 black-and-white photograph, with the relatively well-centered illustration only revealing a modest partiality towards the upper edge as well as a virtually negligible tilt towards that same corner. One of Mickey's spectacular attributes is his near-perfect facial hues, with an abundance of 1951 Bowman Mantles plagued by deep red facial tints. Blistering-sharp edges include four pinpoint corners, and the final exclamation point is a super-clean verso eluding any notable gum stains. Indeed, this museum worthy keepsake has stubbornly defied father-time for three-quarters of a century, with its "heart-stopping" attributes worthy of the highest hobby accolades. Unlike the 1952 Topps Mantle that has already realized some incredible pricing upticks, this offering still retains momentous upside versus its perplexing, undervalued status. Just glancing at this time-defying masterpiece effectively turns back the clock to an era when the "Oklahoma Kid's" mighty round-trippers would validate his unequivocal standing as baseball’s most powerful all-time slugger, with this PSA 8 rookie marvel forever echoing through eternity!

This most eloquent quote was spoken by the legendary CBS sportscaster Heywood Hale Broun when referring to the immortal thoroughbred race horse Secretariat’s supernatural-like ability as well as the mighty Babe Ruth, with both these sports icons exceeding the standard athlete’s expected physical limits. Regarding Goliath-like power, even Mr. Broun would agree that Mickey Charles Mantle stands “heads and heels” above any player who ever stepped into a batter’s box, with “the Mick” potentially capable of testing the confines of even Yellowstone Park! Time after time, his mammoth tape measure blasts would not only outdistance stadium fences, but also their outer perimeters, with this immortal Cooperstown inductee twice blasting home runs off the Yankee Stadium façade. Batting right-handed in 1953, Mantle crushed southpaw Chuck Stobbs fastball at Washington's Griffith Stadium off of the scoreboard and into a neighboring backyard, some 565-feet from home plate. This continues to be the longest "official" home run ever recorded in a Major League game, and even with today's sophisticated conditioning programs, harder throwers, tightly wound baseballs and infinite-like PED usage, no one can come close to matching Mantle's record-setting blast. The unparalleled charm of the ‘52 Topps Mantle is directly linked to Topps Chewing Gum Co. owner Sy Berger’s decision to dump “truckloads” of excess 1952 Topps high-number vending cases into the Atlantic’s murky waters off the coast of New Jersey, prompting the “birth” of the ’52 Topps Mantle’s resounding character. Presented here is subject #5, the awe-inspiring “Babe’s Batting Grip” subject in a BVG GD 2 holder. Seldom surfacing for the taking, you can literally feel the intensity of the “Sultan of Swat’s” legendary batting grip, with his right hand’s pinky finger encompassing the mighty lumber’s knob. description_block: Boasting extremely challenging to find near-perfect centering, this dazzling and recently discovered 1954 Red Heart Mickey Mantle PSA 6 keepsake merits a final resting place in any esteemed Mantle gathering. The 1954 Red Heart 33-subject set was distributed by the John Morrell & Co. manufacturer, regionally distributed with their Red Heart brand dog food. Ultra-desirable for the most meticulous enthusiasts due to their vibrant fire-engine red, bold blue and green colored backgrounds, 11 subjects were issued for each of the three colored series that were evenly distributed throughout the 1954 campaign. Most significantly, the robust hued settings project the super eye pleasing player images to an unprecedented plateau, literally bringing these 72-year-old illustrations to life. As is the case with most post-1950s sets, the most coveted and valuable subject is the immortal Mickey Charles Mantle, and this PSA 6 marvel reveals many of its original factory issued attributes. Of course, it is the “heart-stopping” Mantle pose and near-flawless baby-blue background that “steals the show”, ably assisted by the near-50/50 image positioning. Mild border toning and diminutive corner aging consistent with the assessment are the only notable imperfections. A significant aspect of the hallowed 1954 Mantle Red Heart is, like Stan Musial, no Mantle subject was issued by Topps in their 1954 set due to contractual issues with the Bowman Gum Company. Fresh off the heels of the Yankee's record-setting fifth consecutive world championship, Mantle would once again enjoy an outstanding '54 campaign, walloping 27 round-trippers and knocking in over 100 runs (102) for the first time of his illustrious career. The Mantle Red Heart subject would join forces with his Stahl-Meyer and Bowman mementos as his most popular cards issued during his formidable 1954 season, with the mighty “Mick” embarking on a career that would ultimately place him as an unequivocal baseball icon!

His important rookie card can be said to have inspired the rebirth of enthusiasm for basketball cards. condition_note: Some light soiling and a modest horizontal crease.
special_note: One of the most iconic vintage cards; considered a premier collectible.
description_block: One of the most iconic vintage cards on the planet is the immortal Ty Cobb’s 1914 Cracker Jack #30 specimen, presented here in a resounding SGC FR 1.5 holder. Most significantly, this time-tested candy card treat boasts virtually 50/50 image positioning, with most of these legendary Cracker Jacks plagued by skewed images. The 1914 Cracker Jacks ultra-condition sensitivity stems from the neighboring caramel candy-corn included in their historic 1914 boxes, and this time-defying image has miraculously eluded any unsightly staining or other obtrusive flaws over the past 112 years. The only major technical flaw accounting for the 1.5 assessment is a miniscule pinole situated near the upper right border (affixed on the red setting). Barely visible to the naked eye, this diminutive imperfection does not compromise the heart-stopping aesthetics of the classic “Georgia Peach” central image revealing his iconic “hands apart” batting stance, extremely bold fire-engine red background and near-perfect centering. Some light soling is evident to the left of Cobb’s right shoulder, a modest horizontal crease is found at the lower right border, and some negligible traces of faint candy corn staining on both sides do not detract from the spellbinding aesthetics. The cornerstone Cobb illustration stands right alongside other momentous cardboard images such as the T206 Honus Wagner and 1952 Topps Mantle, proudly revealing itself as one of the hobby’s most revered collectibles. In 1914, card collecting was taken to a new level via the thin stock baseball cardboard subjects inserted into boxes offering the ultra-popular caramel corn. While a myriad of distinguished Hall of Famers and stars were included on the extensive laundry list of baseball’s early 20th century heroes, save Mathewson, Wagner and Joe Jackson, none could possibly compare to the immortal reverence of the Tyrus Raymond Cobb #30 subject. Cobb’s intense facial expression clearly indicates he is ready to wage war against another overmatched twirler, preparing to stroke another one of his 4,189 safeties. It is no secret that Ty Cobb is widely considered one of the finest players who ever graced a baseball diamond. He could hit (his .366 average is still the “best of the best”), run (he stole 891 bases), throw and field better than any player in the “dead-ball” era (with all due respect to Hans Wagner), with Ty’s most amazing achievement being his incomparable run of 12 batting titles in 13 seasons including an extraordinary 9 consecutive titles from 1907-1915. In fact, 1914 would see Tyrus post another league leading average (.368), while also pacing the Junior Circuit in OPS via a stellar .979 mark. No wonder his pre-WWI cardboard remnants are considered premier collectibles, with only a handful of Cobb’s issues possibly achieving the unparalleled stature of a super visually pleasing 1914 Cracker Jack - properly earning a final resting place in PSA’s prestigious “Top 250 Sports Card” periodical. The $166K record-setting sale of an “EX 5” copy in December 2025 put the collecting community on notice as to the unlimited future prosperity of any 1914 Cracker Jack Cobb. Indeed, regardless of any grade, the key concept continues being its overall eye appeal, with this captivating marvel truly residing as one of the finest low-grade examples extant. For nearly 25 years, Cobb ravaged pitchers via his uncanny batting skills, justifying his unequivocal standing as one of baseball’s five 1936 Hall of Fame Charter Members. While many cards of this iconic batsman reveal glorious images, it is his esteemed Cracker Jack that truly boasts the quintessential Cobb batting pose; an unwavering keepsake transcending us back to the early 20th century when the “Georgia Peach” dominated America’s favorite pastime at an unprecedented level!

description_block:
This limited edition (#102/251) OAL Brown baseball is signed by four members of the 1951 World Series champion New York Yankees. 1951 was a watershed year for the New York Yankees, as Joe DiMaggio, one of the greatest players in the game’s history, played his final MLB season. Luckily for the Yankees, a young, Oklahoma-born outfielder named Mickey Mantle made his debut in 1951, showing the world that the Yankees had a ready-made replacement for DiMaggio in center field. A plethora of Hall of Famers, including Yogi Berra, Johnny Mize, and Phil Rizzuto, helped the Yankees claim the American League pennant with a 98-56 record, setting up a cross-town matchup with the New York Giants in the World Series. The Yankees handled the Giants in six games, granting DiMaggio his ninth and third consecutive World Series title.
Hall of Famer Joe DiMaggio signed the sweet spot. Hall of Famer Yogi Berra signed the north panel and inscribed “M.V.P. ’51.” Hall of Famer Phil Rizzuto signed and inscribed “World Series MVP 1951.” Gil McDougald signed the south panel and inscribed “1951 ROY.” The ball exhibits toning. The ball is accompanied by an LOA from JSA for the signatures and inscriptions.
